entries.title: Micah 2:2 "They covet fields, and then seize them
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:2 "They covet fields, and then seize them

They rob a man and his house,

A man and his inheritance" These are four parallel lines with strong VERBS.

  1. "covet" ‒ BDB 326, KB 325, Qal PERFECT with waw
  2. "seize" ‒ BDB 159, KB 186, Qal PERFECT with waw
  3. "take away" ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal PERFECT with waw
  4. "oppress" ‒ BDB 798, KB 897, Qal PERFECT with waw

Remember, the extreme importance that the Jewish people placed on land inheritance within the Promised Land (cf. Lev. 25:23; Num. 33:54; 36:1-12; Josh. 12-21). The land was meant to return to the original owners every fifty years (i.e. Year of Jubilee; see Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.). YHWH's gift to all the descendants of Abraham was now in the hands of greedy, wealthy exploiters. Micah, growing up and living in a small rural community, had seen it again and again.

The term "house" can refer to a place of dwelling or to one's family (as could the term "inheritance"). These exploiters wanted everything—land, children, adults, and all their property!

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry, III. A. #4

entries.title: Micah 2:3 "Therefore, says the Lord,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:3 "Therefore, says the Lord,

Behold, I am planning" The INTERJECTION "behold" (הב, BDB 243 II) denotes a surprising statement of outcome. The UBS Helps For Translators series on Micah, says, "This is a way of showing that something new and unexpected is about to happen" (p. 82).

This is irony. As evil humans plan (same VERB as was used in Micah 2:1, "scheme"), so too, God plans (i.e. "we reap what we sow, e.g. see full list of Scripture texts at Gal. 6:7-10).

▣ "against this family" The term "family" means "clan" (BDB 1046). Notice the aggressive sin of some affects the complacent, silent majority and the whole nation (cf. Amos 3:2) is judged!

▣
NASB  "calamity"
NKJV, TEV, NJB, REB, Peshitta  "disaster"
NRSV, LXX  "evil"
JPSOA  "misfortune"

This Hebrew term (BDB 949) means "evil," "distress," or "wickedness." In Exod. 32:12,14 it refers, as here, to the judgment of God (cf. Deut. 29:112; Amos 9:4). It is used twice in Micah 2:3 and also in Micah 3:2,11.

▣ "you cannot remove your necks" The VERB (BDB 559, KB 561) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT. This idiom of conquest is also used in Lam. 1:14; 5:5. It refers to a yoke on the neck of an ox which directs its activity.

▣ "walk haughtily" This is another IMPERFECT VERB (BDB 229, KB 246). Israel had become proud and arrogant (i.e. see eighth century historical setting in Introduction). God will change their walk and mind about this (cf. Isa. 2:11,12). Here (if literal), it refers to the shameful methods of the Assyrian exile.

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

entries.title: Micah 2:4 "On that day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "On that day" This refers to the time of God's visitation, here of judicial activity, sometimes, as here, it is temporal, other times it is eschatological (i.e. the Day of YHWH.

Special Topic: That Day

▣ "taunt" This refers to a song or proverb (i.e. mashal, BDB 605 II, cf. Hab. 2:6, Peshitta), which others speak to denote the current condition/situation of a person or group. It becomes a training tool for warning others not to do the same.

▣ "lamentation" This refers to a funeral dirge (BDB 624, KB 675, Qal PERFECT). The taunt is Micah 2:4c-f (four lines of poetry).

This term (BDB 624, KB 675) is repeated three times in the Masoretic Hebrew Text:

  1. the VERB (Qal PERFECT with waw)
  2. the NOUN (MASCULINE SINGULAR)
  3. the NOUN (FEMININE SINGULAR)

This repetition denotes a grievous lamentation (wailing).

▣ "We are completely destroyed" This is a COGNATE construction used for emphasis:

  1. BDB 994, KB 1418, a Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  2. BDB 994, KB 1418, a Niphal PERFECT

entries.title: Micah 2:4 "He exchanges the portion of my people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "He exchanges the portion of my people" The term "exchanges" (BDB 558, KB 560, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is a legal term for the transfer of a land title. Thie VERB sounds similar to the VERB in the next line, "removes" (BDB 559, KB 561, Hiphil IMPERFECT).

Verses 4 and 5 are the wail of the powerful, wealthy, influential Israelites (who stole from the poor) over the coming Assyrian exile. But notice, it is not sorrow for their actions, but sorrow over the consequences of their actions. They are reaping what they sowed (in kind)!

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "How He removes it from me!"
TEV  "The Lord has taken our land away"
NJB  "no one else can restore it to them"
REB  "it is taken from us"
JPSOA  "How it slips away from me!"
LXX  "and there was none to prevent him
  from turning away"
Peshitta  "there is none to restore our fields"

The MT is uncertain. Obviously the OBJECT is "the land" (lit. "our fields"). The problem, is the SUBJECT

  1. YHWH
  2. the invader
▣
NASB, Peshitta  "to the apostate"
NKJV  "to a turncoat"
NRSV  "our captors"
TEV  "to those who took us captive"
NJB  "to our despoiler"
REB  "to renegades"
JPSOA  "rebel"
JPSOA (footnote)  "ravager"
NET  "to the conqueror"

The MT has the ADJECTIVE "to apostate" (לשׁובב, BDB 1000), but BDB suggestss reading it as "our captors" (שׁובינו, NET Bible). There is much confusion in how to translate the "proverb" of v. 4. Here is a suggested translation from the UBS Text Project, p. 212:

"He exchanges the inheritance of my people! How will he move (again) towards me, in order to make restitution for the fields which he is distributing?"

"To the apostate He appoints our fields" can refer either to

  1. an apostate (i.e. one who turns back, BDB 1000, NKJV)
  2. JPSOA has "rebel" from "ravager," which denotes the Assyrian invaders (from similar Hebrew root, BDB 1000, NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET Bible).

The irony is that these rich and powerful Israelite land grabbers are calling others (i.e. the invaders) land grabbers.

entries.title: Micah 2:5 "you will have no one stretching a measuring line"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:5 "you will have no one stretching a measuring line" The LXX changes the VERB "exchange" in the previous verse to "measure" to match this line of poetry.

The word "measuring line" (BDB 286) basically means "cord." In context the term can designate

  1. a line/cord used to measure a field, cf. Ps. 78:55; Amos 7:17; or "temple," Zech. 2:2 (i.e. BDB 286, #2)
  2. ones inherited land, cf. Deut. 32:9; Josh. 17:14; 19:9; 1 Chr. 16:18; Ps. 105:11; Ezek. 47:13 (i.e. BDB 286, #3)
  3. measure in preparation to sell
  4. it is used as an idiom of judgment in 2 Sam. 8:2

▣ "For you by lot in the assembly of the Lord" This refers to the sacred division of the Promised Land (Josh. 12-21). This statement is tantamount to the powerful, wealthy, influential being excommunicated from the Promised Land, both temporally and eschatologically (cf. Micah2:10). This passage implies that YHWH's judgment to these exploiters is even more severe than Exod. 20:5; Deut. 5:9 ("visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children"). This exclusion is permanent and transgenerational!

▣ "by lot" The term "lot" (BDB 174) originally referred to the Urim and Thummim carried by the High Priest on his chest behind the twelve stones. It is not certain what form this mechanical means of knowing YHWH's will was:

  1. different colored stones
  2. stones with "yes" or "no" painted on them
  3. stones with letters on them
  4. other unknown means

The NT word for "clergy" comes from this Hebrew concept.

Special Topic: Urim and Thummim

▣ "the assembly of the Lord" This is a covenant phrase. The Septuagint translates the Hebrew term qahal (BDB 874) by the Greek term ecclēsia (gathering or assembly, which was later used by the NT believers as a title for themselves, i.e. church).

Special Topic: Church (ekklēsia)

entries.title: Micah 2:6 "Do not speak out, so they speak out"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:6 "Do not speak out, so they speak out" There is a play (the VERB is repeated three times) on the term "speak out" or "prophesy" (BDB 642, KB 694, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense, i.e "to drop a message on someone," cf. Micah 2:6 [3 times, all Hiphil IMPERFECTS]; Micah2:11 [twice, also Amos 7:16]).

The term "speak out" is literally "to drip" (cf. Deut. 32:2; Ezek. 20:46; 21:2). It possibbly denotes an excited speaking with spittle from the mouth (NET Bible). See Leslis Allen's translation above.

entries.title: Micah 2:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:6-7 Verses 6-7 are dialogue. Micah speaks. It is hard to be certain where Micah starts and stops and where the rich, speaking as a group, start and stop.

 Leslie Allen (New International Commentary on the Old Testament), p. 292, has a good translation of Micah 2:6 and 7: ". . .stop your preaching, they preach. They should stop preaching in this vein: humiliation won't overtake us: the community of Jacob is party to the covenant. Has Yahweh lost His temper? Is this the way He acts? Do not His promises spell good fortune? Do not we keep company with the One who keeps His word?"

 Verses 6 and 7, to some extent, seem to reflect the rich's traditional covenant theology (much like Job's three friends), but it fails to adequately understand the covenant requirements (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-28; 30:15,19; i.e. known as "the two ways," cf. Ps.1).

entries.title: Micah 2:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:7 This verse has three (NASB, NKJV, JPSOA) or four (NRSV, TEV, NJB) questions. Who is speaking is uncertain. Some translations say

  1. the condemned rich of Judah (NET Bible)
  2. a false prophet (NKJV)
  3. YHWH Himself (Jewish Study Bible, p. 1208)

The JPSOA translates the first three poetic lines of v. 7 as follows:

"Is the House of Jacob condemned?"

Is the Lord's patience short?

Is such His practice?"

▣
NASB  "Is it being said, O house of Jacob?"
NKJV  "You who are named the house of Jacob"
NRSV  "Should this be said, O house of Jacob?"
TEV  "Do you think the people of Israel are under
  a curse?"
NJB  "Can the house of Jacob be accursed?"
LXX  "One says, The house of Jacob. . ."
REB  "House of Jacob, can one ask. . .?"
JPSOA  "Is the House of Jacob condemned?"
Peshitta  "That the shame which is spoken against the house
  of Jacob"

The divergence of translations is due to a hapox legommenon, "should it be said" (BDB 55, KB 65, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE). The NET Bible emends it to an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root resulting in, "Does the family of Jacob say?"

The word "accursed" (NJB) or "cursed" (TEV) is the result of an emendation to the term "said."

  1. "Is it said?" ‒ האמור
  2. "Is it cursed?" ‒ הארור

The UBS Text Project, p. 313, gives option #1 a "C" rating, which is their way of saying, "We do not know which is original."

▣ "the Spirit of the Lord" In context this does not refer to the Holy Spirit, but the personality of YHWH (i.e. YHWH's Spirit, cf. Mic. 3:8; Gen. 1:1). Here with the INTERROGATIVE "impatient" (MT, "shortened?"; BDB 894, KB 1126, Qal PERFECT) it refers to the Lord's patience (cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET Bible) or lack of anger (cf. Ps. 103:8-14).

Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit (OT

Special Topic: Spirit in the Bible

Special Topic: The Personhood of the Spirit

▣ Lines 3-5 of verse 8 are difficult to translate in context. Leslie Allen's dynamic equivalent translation in 2:6-7, second paragraph, is helpful. All five lines of v. 8 must be interpreted as a whole.

Remember, Hebrew poetic lines are not always sound plays, but more often, thought parallels.

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry, III.

entries.title: Micah 2:8 "Recently My people have arisen as the enemy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 "Recently My people have arisen as the enemy" The VERB (BDB 877, KB 1086) is a Polel IMPERFECT. The covenant people have repeatedly broken their obligations to the Mosaic Covenant. This is what the exploiters refused to acknowledge! God's people were acting like an invading enemy against their own covenant brothers and sisters (i.e. JPSOA footnote "e").

The problem in translating this phrase is that the MT is using "my people" as the attackers and exploiters, when in the following lines they are the exploited.

Several translations emend the MT to "but you rise up against my people as an enemy" (cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET Bible). See the extended textual note in the UBS Text Project, vol. 5, p. 314.

Special Topic: Covenant

▣ "You strip the robe off a fellow-Israelite" The VERB (BDB 832, KB 980) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT. This reflects the continuing action of the rich in exploiting the poor. This passage reflects the greed and heartlessness of the wealthy, influential, Israelite land grabbers in evicting poor people from their houses and taking their clothes (even their children) as a guarantee for money borrowed (cf. Exod. 22:26,27).

Notice the groups impacted by this exploitation:

  1. covenant brothers, Micah 2:8b-c
  2. military veterans, Micah 2:8d
  3. covenant women, Micah 2:9a-b
  4. covenant children, Micah 2:9c
▣
NASB, JPSOA  "From unsuspecting passers-by"
JPSOA (footnote)  "off peaceful folk"
NKJV  "From those returned from war"
NRSV  "From those who trust you, as they pass by"
TEV  "Men returning from battle, thinking they are
  safe at home, but there you are, waiting
  to steal"
NJB  "on those who feel safe you inflict the damage
  of war"
REB  "from travelers who felt safe"

From these different translations it is obvious that the Hebrew is ambiguous or defective (the LXX and Peshitta reflect a different Hebrew text). From context the "robe" (BDB 971 II) and "mantle" (BDB 12) is demanded from unsuspecting strangers. The phrase about "returned from war" is what causes the confusion.

Two possible interpretations of this ambiguous phrase:

  1. that when Jewish soldiers (JPSOA) returned home from fighting foreign enemies (potential invaders and land grabbers) they thought they were safe, but not so. Their own covenant brothers attacked them unexpectedly and took their land and possessions!
  2. Here is the suggested translation of v. 8 from the UBS Text Project, p. 316.

    "yesterday still my people rose up as an enemy (of God and their poor brothers): (being) in front of a cloak they strip off the honor of those who pass by in confidence, being averse to war/strife."

entries.title: Micah 2:9 "The women of My people you evict"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9 "The women of My people you evict" The VERB (BDB 176, KB 204, Piel IMPERFECT) means "to drive out" (cf. Hosea 9:15). This implies that the husbands have already been sold into indentured servitude, now the wife.

▣ "From her children you take My splendor forever" These children become slaves and worse (as did their parents). Their rightful land inheritance (here called "My splendor") as YHWH's covenant people in the Promised Land (i.e. Year of Jubilee, when land was to be returned to its original tribal owners; see Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.) was lost to greed and exploitation. They will also be corporately affected by the judgment of God (i.e. exile) that will come to national Judah, as it did to Israel. But in the future, they will receive their inheritance again (cf. Micah2:5). So "forever" is a way of showing intensity, not time here.

This may simply be imagery of the policies of the Assyrian army of killing the very young (and the very old) before exiling the parents.

Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios)

entries.title: Micah 2:10 "Arise and go"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10 "Arise and go" These two VERBS (BDB 877, KB 1086, "arise; and BDB 229, KB 246, "go") are both Qal IMPERATIVES. This reflects either

  1. a warning to the faithful few (i.e. the remnant; see Special Topic: Remnant [three senses])
  2. more probably, YHWH's judgment of the nation (i.e. exile)
  3. YHWH speaks to the invaders (NET Bible)

 ▣ "this is no place of rest" This term is used of the Promised Land in Deut. 12:9; Ps. 95:11. Here, it is an idiom for invasion and exile.

▣ "Because of the uncleanness that brings on destruction" This term "uncleanness" (BDB 380) is used in the OT to describe the abominations of the Canaanites. There is some question whether the MT has a VERB (BDB 379 I) or the NOUN (BDB 380). The UBS Text Project gives the VERB an "A" rating. Micah uses this same term to accuse the people of God of similar acts (cf. Lev. 18:24ff) that caused God to remove the Canaanites (cf. Gen. 15:12-21). He now removes the Israelites.

This verse has another COGNATE construction:

  1. VERB, BDB 287 II, KB 285, Piel IMPERFECT ("bring a destruction")
  2. NOUN, BDB 287, KB 285 ("a painful destruction")

Special Topic: Abomination (OT), #2

▣
NASB  "painful destruction"
NKJV  "utter destruction"
NRSV, Peshitta  "grievous destruction"
TEV  "doom this place to destruction"
NJB  "extortionate pledge"
REB  "any mischief however cruel"
JPSOA  "terrible destruction shall befall"
LXX  "you were corrupted with corruption"

The Niphal PARTICIPLE (BDB 599, KB 637) is literally "made sick" (e.g. Jer. 14:17). Physical illness is used as imagery for sin and rebellion (e.g. Micah1:9; Isa. 1:5-6; Ps. 103:3; Isa. 53:5).

entries.title: Micah 2:11 "If a man, walking after the wind and falsehood"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:11 "If a man, walking after the wind and falsehood" This seems to refer to the message of the false prophets who are readily embraced, while true prophets are rejected (cf. Micah 2:6). These false teachers were always preaching covenant health, wealth, and prosperity (cf. Micah 3:5; based on proof-texts from Deut. 27-29). They always ignored the covenant responsibilities (see The Disease of the Health, Wealth Gospels by Gordon Fee). Most OT covenants are conditional! See Special Topic: Covenant

This phrase is a play on the words "spirit" and "wind" (BDB 924, cf. Hosea 8:7, 12:1). See Special Topic: Breath, Wind, Spirit (OT)

▣ "I will speak out to you concerning wine and liquor" This would refer to

  1. God's agricultural abundance, promised in Deuteronomy 28
  2. here, it may refer to the spiritual effects of prosperity (cf. Isa 5:11,12,22; 28:7)
  3. drunkenness is often imagery for judgment in the OT

Special Topic: Biblical Attitudes Toward Alcohol and Alcohol Abuse, II, A. #5

▣ "He would be spokesman to this people" The message of the prosperity made promises to the covenant people (Deut. 28), but separated or never mentioned the covenant responsibility (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27; 29). This was a favorite theme (as it is today). These false teachers promised peace (cf. Micah3:5) and prosperity, but in reality, God's judgment, not blessing, was swiftly approaching!

entries.title: Micah 2:12 "I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:12 "I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 62, KB 74) for the "surety of YHWH's promise" of return and covenant blessing. This is a promise of future restoration to the Promised Land through YHWH's power by YHWH Himself (cf. Deut. 30:4; Jer. 23:3; 31:8). Even though Israel was judged because of the wicked, all of its people paid the price of invasion and exile. God will set it straight for those (and their descendants) who truly trust and obey Him (i.e. the faithful remnant)!

Verse 12 is in the first person ("I"), but Micah 2:13 is in the third person. This is common in Hebrew, but here, possibly Micah 2:12 is YHWH speaking and Micah 2:13 Micah's comment and development.

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "the remnant of Israel" This theological concept becomes a recurrent hope in the Prophets. It refers to a small group of faithful, believing, obedient, covenant Israelites from which YHWH will build His kingdom (cf. Micah 4:6-7). The majority of the covenant people (i.e. descendants of Abraham) are not believers, not obedient, and not right with God. They deserve temporal and eschatological judgment.

Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses)

▣  "like sheep in the fold,

Like a flock in the midst of its pasture" This may be a play on

  1. a place name, Bozrah (MT, JPSOA, BDB 131 II), which was known for its excellent sheep
  2. a parallel to a pasture and, therefore, a protected enclosure (BDB 131 I, found only here in the OT, i.e. sheepfold, which requires an emendation to the MT using an Arabic root, "in a fold")
  3. other options, the LXX has "like sheep in affliction"; Peshitta, "like sheep when they are in danger." This option is also followed by the Latin Vulgate.

These allusions to sheep and shepherding are covenant imagery for YHWH's care and provision (cf. Psalm 23; also Messianic in John 10). The sheep are guarded and cared for. The last line of Micah 2:12 seems to imply

  1. a joyful group
  2. as in NKJV and NIV, a large number of people

entries.title: Micah 2:12-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:12-13 These verses are a radical change from judgment to hope, which characterizes this book. There have been several theories concerning this radical change:

  1. John Calvin and Kimchi see Micah 2:12 and 13 as referring to the deportation into exile
  2. it is possibly another quote from the false teachers (i.e. a response to Micah 2:10; Ibn Ezra)
  3. this is Micah's personal hope in YHWH's protection (Aramaic Targums)
  4. YHWH or Davidic Messiah as the good faithful Shepherd (i.e. Ps. 23; John 10)
  5. an insertion of the later redactor
  6. I prefer the sudden shifts to the poetic parallelism known as antithetical parallelism, so common in Hebrew Wisdom Literature, and prophetic poetry.

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry

entries.title: Micah 2:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:13 Micah seems to be speaking again (i.e. third person references to YHWH). This verse is Messianic text. The Davidic kingship will be restored (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17).

There is a word play between "breaker" (Micah 2:13a, BDB 829, KB 971, Qal PARTICIPLE) and "break out" (Micah 2:13b, BDB 829, KB 971, Qal PERFECT). The king will lead his people out of the pen of the exile into a large pasture, where they run and jump with joy!

Notice the concept of pen is used in two senses:

  1. in Micah 2:12 as a protective enclosure
  2. in Micah 2:13 as a restrictive enclosure

Notice how the Davidic King (cf. Micah 2:13c) is paralleled with YHWH (cf. Micah 2:13d). This implies a divine king (cf. Micah 5:2-4)! However, this context could be seen as YHWH, the One who caused the exile is the very One who reverses it. The king may be a way of referring to YHWH (cf. Micah 4:7; 1 Sam. 8:7).

Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

▣ "the gate" This was Old Testament imagery for the power of a city or city-state. This is a word play between the gate of the sheepfold and the national power (i.e. Assyria), which exiled the Northern Ten Tribes (in 722 B.C.).

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Micah 3:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:1 This is a strong contrast to Micah 2:12-13. The abrupt transition from judgment to restoration characterizes this book. This literary technique may be unconsciously related to the antithetical parallelism of Hebrew poetry! Chapter 3 picks up again on the theme of Divine judgment from Micah 2.

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry

▣ "Hear" This is the Hebrew Shema (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE), which means to hear so as to do (cf. Micah 1:2; 3:1; 6:1). This word seems to outline the book. See note at Micah 1:2.

Special Topic: Listen/Hear (shema)

▣  ". . .heads of Jacob

And rulers of the house of Israel.

Is it not for you to know justice" All three lines of poetry refer to the political leaders of Judah (cf. Micah 3:9-10) who should have been trained in the Mosaic law (cf. Deut. 12:17), but followed a policy of greed and self-centeredness (cf. Amos 5:15; Isa. 1:16,17). Calling Judah, Israel, probably shows

  1. this was spoken after the fall of the Northern Ten Tribes to Assyria in 722 B.C.
  2. it was a way of showing condemnation (e.g. Ezekiel 23)
  3. Israel was the colletive term for all the tribes before the split in 922 B.C.
    Special Topic: Israel (the name)

▣ "justice" See Special Topic: Justice

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BRIEF OUTLINE OF THE CHAPTER ‒ YHWH calls the evil leaders of Judah to account.

  1. Political rulers, Micah 3:1-4

  2. Prophets, Micah 3:5-8
    1. false prophets described in Micah 3:5-7
    2. true prophets described in Micah 3:8

  3. Civil rulers, priests, and prophets are addressed collectively, Micah 3:9-12

  4. There is an obvious parallelism between A. and C. (i.e. "hear," shema, Qal IMPERATIVE; see Special Topic: Listen/Hear (shema))

  5. See full outline in Introduction VII.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Micah 3:2 "You who hate good and love evil"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:2 "You who hate good and love evil" The two VERBS "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338) and "love" (BDB 12, KB 17) are both Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLES. These leaders' response was exactly opposite from YHWH's will (cf. Isa. 1:16-17, 21-23, 26; 5:7,8,20; Amos 5:15; note Jesus' words in Matt. 6:23).

entries.title: Micah 3:2-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:2-3 Instead of acting like shepherds, these political leaders (cf. Ezekiel 34) acted like butchers (i.e. "tear off," "strip off," "break," "chop").

  1. "tear off" ‒ BDB 159, KB 186, Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Micah 2:8; 7:2,3
  2. "strip off" ‒ BDB 832, KB 980, Hiphil PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 34:2,3
  3. "break" ‒ BDB822, KB 953, Piel PERFECT
  4. "chop: ‒ BDB 831, KB 975, Qal PERFECT, cf. Ezek. 11:3,6,7

The phrase, "eat the flesh of my people," is used in a figurative sense in Ps. 14:4, 27:2 and Prov. 30:14.

entries.title: Micah 3:4 "Then they will cry out to the Lord,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:4 "Then they will cry out to the Lord,

But He will not answer them" The VERB "cry out" (BDB 227, KB 277, Qal IMPERFECT) is a legal term for appealing to the court for help.

  1. as these wicked judges did not hear the cries of the poor aliens, orphans, and widows
  2. God will not hear their cry either (cf.Deut. 31:17,18; 32:20; Prov. 21:13; Isa. 1:15; 59:2; 64:7; Jer. 33:5; James 2:13)

▣ "He will hide His face from them at that time" The VERB (BDB 711, KB 771, Hiphil) is JUSSIVE in form, but not in meaning.

The "them" refers to the faithless leaders. This is ultimate rejection.

  1. "He will not answer them," v. 4
  2. "He will hide His face from them" (cf. Deut. 31:17; Isa. 1:15)
  3. The Aramaic Targums translate this as YHWH remembering His shekinah glory
    Special Topic: Shekinah

▣ "Because they have practiced evil deeds" Here is the problem. YHWH's people have repeatedly and flagrantly rebelled and rejected their covenant obligations (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28). They are now reaping what they sowed (cf. Micah 7:13; Isa. 3:10,11; see full list of Scripture parallels at Gal. 6:7-10).

entries.title: Micah 3:5 "Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:5 "Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets" The prophets were one of several ways to know the will of YHWH. The very ones who were to reveal YHWH, did not know Him (cf. Hosea 4:1). 1 Sam. 28:6 mentions three ways Saul inquired of YHWH:

  1. dreams, visions
  2. Urim and Thummim (i.e. High Priest)
  3. prophet (i.e. Samuel)

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

Special Topic: Ways of Revelation

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT), I. B. #3

▣ "Who lead my people astray" The VERB (BDB 1073, KB 1766, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) means "to cause to err" (cf. Amos 2:4; Hosea 4:12; 2 Kgs. 21:9; Isa. 3:12; 9:16; Jer. 50:6). This refers to the false prophets mentioned in Micah 2:6-7; 3:10-11.

▣ "When they have something to bite with their teeth" This refers to the eating of food (i.e. gifts from the people they prophesied for, cf. Micah 3:5, lines 4 and 5). They prophesy for hire, not for God (cf. Isa. 59:9-11). They tell

  1. the generous clients just what they want to hear (i.e. peace and prosperity)
  2. their poor clients problems and scarcity

The term "bite" (BDB 675, KB 729, Qal PARTICIPLE) usually refers to a snake bite.

▣ "They cry, 'Peace'" Literally shalom (BDB 1022) is the Hebrew word which means "wholeness." Apparently,

  1. if the prophets were well-fed (i.e. paid in food, cf. 1 Sam. 9:7-8), they would proclaim good news (e.g. Jer. 5:12; 6:13-14; 8:10-11; 13:14; 23:17; Ezek. 13:10)
  2. if they were not well-fed, they would proclaim "holy war" (BDB 536)

Their message was based on selfish interests, not YHWH's will. These prophets were available for private, as well as, royal consultations.

However, giving a gift to a prophet was a common practice (e.g. 1 Kgs. 14:3; 2 Kgs. 4:42; 8:8-9). It is the manipulation of the message that is the problem!

Special Topic: Peace (OT, shalom)

▣ "They declare holy war" The term "holy" is not in the MT, but comes from the VERB (BDB 872, KB 1073, Piel PERFECT with waw), which comes from the Hebrew root for "holy." It is used to describe setting apart certain people for war in Jer. 51:27; Joel 3:9 and here (cf. Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, p. 177).

The implication is that God will send bad things, problems, conflicts against those who are not generous with the prophets (i.e. YHWH's spokesperson). I sense this same technique today in tithing sermons that pronounce doom if you do not give a set percentage to the speaker or church (i.e. storehouse tithing)!

Special Topic: Tithing

entries.title: Micah 3:6 "night. . .darkness. . .sun will go down. . .day will become dark"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:6 "night. . .darkness. . .sun will go down. . .day will become dark" These are four terrible images (no sunlight used by Isaiah) for the removal of God's Spirit and insight from the rulers and prophets.

Darkness is used as imagery for lack of revelation (i.e. light, e.g. Ps. 82:5; Prov. 2:13; 4:19; Isa. 59:9; 2 Pet. 1:19; 1 John 1:6; 2:11). The darkness will result in judgment (cf. Amos 5:18-20; another similar image in Amos 8:11-12 is famine of God's word).

YHWH will not respond to

  1. their prayers
  2. their prophets

Special Topic: Darkness, I.

▣ "vision" Visions (BDB 302) and dreams (BDB 321) were often paralleled (cf. Job 33:15; Isa. 29:7; Dan. 7:1) as ways of receiving YHWH's message. Usually (but not exclusively) visions occurred in the day and dreams at night.

Special Topic: Ways of Revelation

▣ "divination" This (BDB 890, KB 1115) was an ancient means of knowing and effecting the future through some physical or mechanical means (e.g. negative, Deut. 18:9-22; positive, 1 Sam. 28:6 and Gen. 44:5,15). Divination is mankind's attempt to conrol their own lives instead of trusting YHWH.

Special Topic: Divination

entries.title: Micah 3:7 "seers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:7 "seers" This was the earliest name for prophets (BDB 302, e.g. 1 Sam. 9:9; 2 Sam. 24:11; 1 Chr. 9:22; 25:5; Isa. 30:10; Amos 7:12).

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT), I. B.

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "ashamed"
NRSV, TEV, LXX  "disgraced"
NJB  "covered with shame"
REB  "overcome with shame"
JPSOA  "shall be shamed"

The VERB (BDB 101, KB 116, Qal PERFECT with waw) means to be ashamed (e.g. Micah 7:16; Hosea 4:19; 10:6; 13:15 and many times in Isaiah).

Special Topic: Shame

▣
NASB  "embarrassed"
NKJV  "abashed"
NRSV  "put to shame"
TEV  "humiliated"
NJB  "covered with confusion"
JPSOA, Peshitta  "confounded"
LXX  "mocked"

This VERB (BDBb 340, Qal PERFECT with waw) is parallel with "ashamed" and also means ashamed. They are both used together in Isa. 24:23. It is used of

  1. idolaters in Isa. 1:29
  2. diviners, here
  3. Babylon in Jer. 50:12

▣ "they will all cover their mouths" Literally this is "mustache" (BDB 974). This symbol of covering the mustache meant

  1. grief (cf. Ezek. 24:17,22)
  2. shame (i.e. lepers, Lev. 13:45)

▣ "Because there is no answer from God" These leaders are suffering the same lack of communication with God as the leaders described in Micah 3:4 (cf. 1 Sam. 28:6). Heaven is silent!

entries.title: Micah 3:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:8 As verses 5-7 have been a discussion of false (LXX) prophets (cf. Amos 8:11-12), Micah 3:8 is a description of a true prophet who is in full communication with YHWH (cf. Ps. 89:13-14, the true prophet shares, or better reflects, the character of God).

Notice the true prophet is filled (BDB 569, KB 583, Qal PERFECT) with

  1. power (BDB 470)
  2. YHWH's Spirit (cf. Isa. 11:2; Ezek. 2:2)
  3. justice (BDB 1048 "judgment")
  4. courage (BDB 150 "might") to make sin known (cf. Isa. 58:1)

What a contrast with the leaders' shame, grief, and impotence!

Although the full doctrine of the indwelling Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity, is not obvious in the OT, the personal presence of God with and within humans is revealed:

  1. Bezalel, Exod. 31:3; 35:31
  2. Joshua, Deut. 34:9
  3. Saul, 1 Sam. 19:23-24
  4. Elijah, 1 Kgs. 18:46
  5. Ezekiel, Ezek. 1:3; 37:1; 40:1
  6. Micah, Micah 3:8
  7. Messiah, Isaiah 11:2; 48:16; 61:1 (Luke 4:18-19)

As evil indwells humans, so too, the personal presence of YHWH. Fallen humans are directed and/or influenced by one of two spiritual forces.

Special Topic: Spirit in the Bible

Special Topic: The Personhood of the Spirit

Special Topic: The Trinity

▣
NASB  "On the other hand"
NKJV, Peshitta  "but truly"
NRSV, TEV  "but as for me"
NJB  "No so with me"
REB  "But I am"
JPSOA  "But I"
LXX  "otherwise"

Literally the MT has "but indeed I." The Hebrew ADVERB (BDB 19) is a strong ADVERSATIVE (used often in Job, cf. Micah 1:11; 11:5; 12:7; 13:4; 14:18; 17:10; 33:1).

▣ "Jacob. . .Israel" As the last two lines of Micah 3:8 show Micah addressing both Judah's sins and Israel's sins, so too, lines 1 and 2 of Micah 3:9. It is often difficult to know if Micah is addressing Israel, Judah, or both by these two collective names.

Special Topic: Israel (the name)

3:9
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "Now hear this"
NRSV, JPSOA  "hear this"
TEV  "listen to me"
NJB  "kindly listen to this"
REB  "Listen to this"
LXX  "Do hear this"

This phrase is literally "hear I pray this."

  1. The VERB (BDB 1033, KB 1570) is a Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. followed by a PARTICLE used for entreaty (בא)
  3. the DEMONSTRATIVE ADJECTIVE "this"

▣ "Who abhor justice" The VERB (BDB 1073, KB 1765, Piel PARTICIPLE) means regard as an abomination (e.g. Amos 5:10; 6:8; Isa. 14:19; 49:7). These leaders were not sincerely wrong, but haters of the right, good, and godly (cf. Isa. 5:20; Amos 6:12).

The term "justice" (BDB 1048) is repeated in Micah 3:8 and 9.

Special Topic: Justice

▣ "And twist everything that is straight" The VERB "twist" (BDB 786, KB 875, Piel IMPERFECT) means "to pervert" or "to make crooked" (cf. Prov. 10:9; 28:18; Isa. 59:8).

The term "straight" is the etymological root of the OT term for "justice" or "righteousness," which meant a straight edge or measuring reed (cf. Isa. 5:20). Most of the Hebrew words for sin speak of a deviation from this Divine standard.

Special Topic: Righteousness

entries.title: Micah 3:10 "Zion. . .Jerusalem"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:10 "Zion. . .Jerusalem" Zion is the name of one of the seven hills upon which Jerusalem was built. It often is used to refer to the whole city or nation. This must be Judah.

Special Topic: Zion

▣ "with bloodshed. . .with violent injustice" These two NOUNS are parallel (cf. Jer. 22:13,17; Hab. 2:12).

entries.title: Micah 3:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:11 All three groups of leaders are mentioned in this verse and all three are condemned for their greedy, materialistic attitude (cf. Micah 7:3; Isa. 56:9-12; Jer. 5:30-31; 6:13-14; 8:8-12; 14:13-18,22-23; 26:10-15,16; Ezek. 13; 22:23-31).

▣ "pronounce judgment for a bribe" This shows the corruption of the judiciary (cf. Micah 7:3; 2 Chr. 19:7; Isa. 1:23; 5:23). Wealth controlled every aspect of the covenant peoples' life.

Special Topic: Wealth

▣ "priests instruct for a price" One role of the priests (and Levites) was to educate the people on the precepts of the Mosaic Law (e.g. Deut. 33:10; 2 Chr. 15:3; 17:9). Priestly understanding and teaching (and living) of the Mosaic Law was crucial to a healthy, spiritual Israel (cf. Hosea 4:6). But, here they educate only for a price (cf. Micah 3:5).

Special Topic: Levitical Priests

▣ "Yet they lean on the Lord, saying" The term "lean" is used of leaning on a staff (BDB 1043, KB 1612, Niphal IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 23:4). These leaders were wrapping their evil deeds in religious dress. Their mouth said one thing; their actions another (cf. Isa. 29:13)! They were claiming YHWH's protection (covenant benefit) because of their covenant relationship to Him, but were completely ignoring the covenant requirements (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 27-29; Isa. 6:9-10; 29:13). The Mosaic Covenant was conditional!

▣ "Calamity will not come upon us" This must have been a recurrent theme of the false prophets, which became a cultural proverb (cf. Jer. 5:12; 23:17; Amos 9:10), but they were wrong (cf. Micah 2:3).

entries.title: Micah 3:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:12 This must have been an extremely startling statement to the people of Judah. They trusted in YHWH's promises that Jerusalem and the temple would never fall (i.e. Isaiah's promises to Hezekiah, probably based in 2 Samuel 7), and yet, because of their flagrant neglect of the ethical aspects of the covenant, YHWH would take them into exile. Jerusalem would be like Samaria (cf. Micah 1:6)! This is the first prophetic mention of the fall of Jerusalem ("plowed as a field") and the temple (i.e. overgrown with vegetation, literally "a high place of a forest"). This is theologically parallel to Isaiah 5. This verse is quoted in Jer. 26:18 during Jeremiah's trial for false prediction.

I am sure that Micah was discredited in 701 B.C. when this did not occur (i.e. Sennacherib's army destroyed by YHWH, cf. 2 Kgs. 19:35-37), however, the prophet was vindicated in 586 B.C. when this prophecy was literally fulfilled under the siege of Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, asserts that the king (i.e. Hezekiah, cf. Micah 1:1) and people of Judah responded to Micah's message and, therefore, God relented of His judgment (p. 36). Hezekiah's repentance is recorded in 2 Kgs. 20:1-7.

▣ "on account of you" They (the political and religious leaders) were not only going to experience the judgment of YHWH (like the wealthy exploiters), their activities were the reason for the judgment of God!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What was the essence of the false prophets' message in Micah 2:6-11?
  2. Why is Micah 2:12-13 such a radical break from the context?
  3. How does one tell the difference between a false prophet and a true prophet?
  4. How can God promise to always have a man on the Davidic throne (2 Samuel 7), and yet predict the total destruction of Jerusalem and the monarchy?

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:1,3-5 Notice the different speakers. This entire section is very similar to Isa. 2:2-4.

  1. These are words from Micah, as are Micah 4:9-13.
  2. In Micah 4:2 the nations speak,
  3. In Micah 4:6-8 YHWH speaks.
4:1
NASB  "In the last days"
NKJV, Peshitta  "In the latter days"
NRSV, REV, TEV, JPSOA  "In the days to come"
NJB  "But in the days to come"
NET  "In the future"
LXX  "As at the last days"

This phrase (BDB 31 [KB 35 I, #2] CONSTRUCT with BDB 398) is repeated often in the OT (cf. Gen. 49:1; Num. 24:14; Deut. 4:30; 31:29; Isa. 2:2; Jer. 23:20; 30:24; 48:47; 49:39; Ezek. 38:16; Dan. 10:14; Hosea 3:5; Micah 4:1).

BDB describes it in this way, "The final period of history so far as the speaker's perspective reaches. It often equals the ideal or Messianic future."

The phrase has some variation:

  1. Dan. 2:28 ‒ BDB 1079 CONSTRUCT with BDB 1095 ("the end of days")
  2. Ezek. 38:8 ‒ BDB 31 CONSTRUCT with BDB 1040 ("the latter years")
  3. also in Ezekiel 38 the phrase is parallel to the famous prophetic phrase "that day" (cf. Ezek. 30:2-3; 38:10,14,18; 39:11; also Isa. 2:12; 10:3; 13:6,9; 34:2,8; 61:2; Jer. 30:7,8; Joel 1:15; 2:11,31; Amos 5:18; Zeph. 1:14, 15, 16,18).

The rabbis of the interbiblical period developed a concept of two ages: the current evil age (begun in Genesis 3) and an age of righteousness inaugurated by the Messiah (cf. Micah 3:12-13; 5:1-5a). However, from further NT revelation (i.e. progressive revelation), we understand that the Messiah came not once, but twice (see Special Topic below). The period from the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem until a Coming could be called the "last days."

The interpretive issue is when does this Coming occur?

  1. some temporal future coming (i.e. A.D. 70)
  2. before an earthly thousand year reign
  3. before the beginning of eternity?

Part of this question deals with how we view the future. Is it earth-like (restored Garden of Eden, i.e. Genesis 1-2; Revelation 21-22; see Special Topic: Eden) or totally different (cf. 1 Cor. 15:35-49)? Is the Bible literal (dispensational premillennial) or literary (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruninghooks)?

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT), III., IV., and VI.

Special Topic: That Day

Special Topic: Second Coming, IV.

Special Topic: This Age and the Age to Come

Special Topic: The Last Days

Special Topic: Apocalyptic Literature

▣ "the mountain of the house of the Lord" Jerusalem was built on seven hills. The two major ones were Mt. Moriah, on which the temple stood, and Mt. Zion (i.e. site of the old Jebusite fortress and David's palace; see Special Topic: Zion), which became literary imagery for the whole city (cf. Micah 4:2).

The imagery of a mountain as the dwelling place of the gods is recurrent in Mesopotamian, Canaanite, and even YHWH (cf. Ps. 48:2; 87; Isa. 14:13; Ezek. 28:14), and Greco-Roman literature.

There is an interesting article, "Divine Assembly," in Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, pp. 50-53 and also "Mountain" (pp. 572-574). See Special Topic: Heavenly Council of Angelic Beings

  1. for Mesopotamia ‒ ziggurats (man-made mountains)
  2. for Canaan ‒ Mt. Zaphon
  3. for Hebrews
    1. Mt. Sinai
    2. Mt. Moriah/Zion
    3. "the mountain in the north" (i.e. Ps. 48:1-2; Isa. 14:13)
  4. for Greeks ‒ Mt. Olympus

Earlier Micah has just predicted the total destruction of Jerusalem and the temple (cf. Micah 3:12). Now he asserts that YHWH's universal kingdom will come to fruition in Jerusalem. He will establish His reign on a renamed Mt. Zion (i.e. "New Jerusalem," cf. Rev. 21; see full exegetical notes online). The ruined hill will become the most important mountain on the earth (note the parallelism between lines 2, 3, and 4).

For the difference between OT prophecies about the future and NT prophecies, see full note at Micah 4:7 or Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

▣ "It will be raised above the hills" This is figurative language representing the preeminence of the temple in Jerusalem. Always Jewish people say, "Let us go up to Jerusalem." This concept is now widened into a universal sense. Mt. Moriah is viewed as the highest, most significant elevation on the planet, that place that is closest to God!

▣ "the peoples will stream to it" Notice this wonderful universal element in Micah 4:1-3. This is a recurrent theme in the OT (cf. Ps. 22:27; 66:4; 86:9; Isa. 2:2-4; 19:21,23; 27:13; 45:22-23; 50:6-8; 66:23; Jer. 3:17; 4:2; Zech. 2:11; 8:20-23; 14:16). See Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Notice how in the OT people come to God's mountain on the temple, but in the NT His people are sent out (Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8). There is a new temple—Jesus (cf. John 2:19,21)—and by faith in Him each believer becomes a temple (cf. 1 Cor. 6:19). Instead of coming to the temple in Jerusalem, the NT temples go to the nations! God's universal, eternal, redemptive plan is now functioning!

Notice the startling contrast between Micah 3:12 (i.e. exile) and Micah 4:l (i.e. restoration and glorification). Also notice the universal nature of the coming reign of the Messiah (cf. Micah 2:13; 5:2-5a). This universal aspect is so characteristic of Isaiah and Micah (as well as Dan. 2:45; 7:9-10,13-14).

It is uncertain if the nations

  1. come once and go home
  2. come every year like a Jewish annual feast

It is to be noted that in a context of Neo-Babylonian exile (cf. Micah 4:10); the VERB "will stream" (BDB 625, KB 676, Qal PERFECT with waw), is the same VERB Qal IMPERFECT) used to describe the captive nations streaming away from Babylon in Jer. 51:44. Cyrus (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:3), YHWH's chosen vessel, allowed all the exiled people to return home and funded the rebuilding of their national temples.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BACKGROUND STUDY

  1. Micah 4:1-3 is very similar to Isa. 2:2-3. It is obvious that literary borrowing has occurred from one or the other or they both borrowed from a third source.

  2. This chapter (vv. 1-8) wonderfully predicts the fulfillment of Gen. 3:15. The redemption and fellowship of all peoples with their Creator is clearly asserted (cf. Isa. 2:23; and Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan).
     But before this great day, tragedy and judgment on Israel and Judah will occur by divine decree (cf. vv. 9-12; also note Dan. 9:24-27). However, YHWH will empower His people to overcome their enemies (i.e. in this context, Assyria and Neo-Babylon, cf. v. 13).

  3. The book of Micah seems to reflect two historical dates, as well as an eschatological position. Throughout the book, either
    1. the Syro-Ephramatic War (i.e. the military alliance of Syria and Israel) of 735 B.C. is the background
    2. the invasion of Judah by Sennacherib the Assyrian King in 701 B.C. However, at the beginning of chapter 4, we realize that these two historical crises foreshadowed
      1. the later Neo-Babylonian invasions of Judah (Micah 4:10) occurred in 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.
      2. the ultimate crisis of history, the Kingdom of God vs. the kingdom of evil. See my exegetical notes on Matt. 24 and the book of Revelation (2024).
    3. Several questions are left unanswered!
      1. Does any OT prophet see the two comings of the Messiah?
      2. Does this refer to
         (1) a Jewish oriented millennium
         (2) a church oriented eternity?
      3. Are the nations becoming believers and followers of YHWH (Micah 4:1-4) and/or His Messiah or are they enemies to the bitter end (Micah 4:11-13)?
    4. Books that have been very helpful to me in trying to interpret prophecy in its historical setting are
      1. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the OT
      2. Douglas Stuart and Gordon Fee, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth, pp. 181-204
      3. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic
        Special Topic: Prophecy (OT), VI.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Micah 4:2 "And many nations will come and say"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:2 "And many nations will come and say" Verse 2 records the supposed comment of the nations. All people are welcome (e.g. Isa. 11:10; 49:22).

  1. if there is one God (i.e. monotheism, cf. 1 Kgs. 8:43,60)
  2. all humans are made in His image (cf. Gen. 1:26-27)
  3. He promises to redeem all mankind (cf. Gen. 3:15)
  4. then "one people" is the ultimate goal (cf. Gal. 3:23-29; Eph. 2:11-3:13). YHWH chose to reveal Himself through national Israel, but ultimately through the ideal Israelite, His Servant (cf. Isa. 52:13-53:12), His Son (cf. Psalm 2; 2 Samuel 7)

Verse 2 has several IMPERATIVES:

  1. "come" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "go" ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT
  3. "teach" ‒ BDB 434, KB 436, Hiphil IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning
  4. "walk" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal COHORTATIVE

The term "many" (cf. vv. 2,3) in the Bible often has the connotation of "all" (i.e. this is the context of Micah 3:1-3).

  1. Isaiah 53
    1. "all," v. 6, lines 1 and 3
    2. "many," vv. 11d and 12e
  2. Romans 5
    1. v. 18, "all"
    2. v. 19, "many"

Special Topic: Monotheism

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

Special Topic: Messiah

▣  "That he may teach us about His ways

And that we may walk in His paths" There are three aspects to biblical faith (cf. Ezra 7:10):

  1. knowing God (personal relationship)
  2. knowing God's will (Scripture, cf. Ps. 19:7-14; 119:1-176)
  3. living God's will (Scripture obedience, cf. Isa. 51:4-8)

This is like an OT Great Commission (compare Matt. 28:19-20, especially v. 20).

YHWH wants a people who reflect His character. His goal has always been to reach the world (cf. lines 6 & 7)! Humans were created for fellowship with God (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:8)!

This is the opposite of Micah 3:6-7. Revelation is restored!

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

Special Topic: Terms for God's Revelation

entries.title: Micah 4:3 "And he will judge between many peoples"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:3 "And he will judge between many peoples" This is an extreme contrast between Judah's judicial actions and YHWH's (cf. Micah 3:1, 9, 11). YHWH's judgments (i.e. Messiah's judgments [so Ibn Ezra], Isa. 11:3-5; Micah 5:4) will result in social peace, not exploitation (cf. Isa. 2:2-4).

▣  "Then they will hammer their swords into plowshares

And their spears into pruning hooks" This is beautiful imagery to describe the peaceful reign of the Messiah (i.e. note the synonymous parallelism of the next line of poetry, cf. Micah 5:5a; Ps. 46:9, 76:3; Hosea 2:18; for the reverse imagery see Joel 3:10).

 The exact nature of these agricultural implements is uncertain (BDB 88 III). They were made of metal and were used, not like a wooden plow to turn over soil, but to scratch a furrow. It was usually a metal tipped piece of sharpened wood.

Special Topic: Messianic Era

▣ "And never again will they train for war" The VERB "train" (BDB 540, KB 531, Qal IMPERFECT) means to learn (e.g. Deut. 4:10; 17:19; Ps. 119:73). It can refer to warfare (cf. 1 Chr. 5:18; Song of Songs 3:8). Not only is the coming restoration universal, it is also permanent (cf. Micah 4:5 line 3; 7 line 4).

entries.title: Micah 4:4 "And each of them will sit under his vine
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:4 "And each of them will sit under his vine

And under his fig tree" Israel and Judah were agricultural societies. This idiom denoted a peaceful and happy agricultural life. These phrases reflect the restoration of all the covenant descendants of Abraham back to the Promised Land, where each had their family land given by lot in Josshua 12-19 restored (cf. 1 Kgs. 4:25; Isa. 36:16; Zech. 3:10). This was meant to be a regular event (i.e. Year of Jubilee), but God's people never implemented it.

Special Topic: Feasts of Israel, II. C.

▣ "With no one to make them afraid" In the OT if God's people live in light of His promises and covenant (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28), He will defend them (cf. Lev. 26:3-6).

This text in Micah reflects the Messiah's presence and rule (which reflects an eschatological setting).

▣ "For the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken" This speaks of the power and trustworthiness of YHWH's Word (cf. Isa. 40:5,8; 45:23; 55:11). His promises and trustworthiness are the basis of mankind's hope and faith (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:56).

The title, "Lord of hosts," in a context relates to Israel and Judah. YHWH is the commander and leader of the army of angels (i.e. Josh. 5:13-15). In some contexts (i.e. Mesopotamian astral worship) "hosts" refers to the pagan theory of gods/angels behind the lights in the sky (i.e. planets, stars, constellations, comets, etc.) that control human lives.

Special Topic: Anthropomorphic Language to Describe God

Special Topic: Angels in the Bible

Special Topic: Lord of Hosts

entries.title: Micah 4:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:5 This verse seems to be out of context. This is a strange verse in a context which speaks of the universal and permanent reign of the one true God, YHWH of Israel. Some see it as:

  1. This glorious future is not here yet because currently every nation has its own god (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:29).
  2. Not all people of all the nations would recognize YHWH even in a future ideal time (e.g. Rev. 22:15).
  3. This is an affirmation of those from the nations who have come to Jerusalem (cf. Micah 4:1e, 2a, 3a,b) and now affirm YHWH their sovereign and God forever.

The tension in this chapter between "believing nations" and "unbelieving nations" is seen in the contrast between Micah 4:1-4 and Micah 4:5!

Special Topic: "The Name" of YHWH (OT)

Special Topic: Seek the Lord

Special Topic: Call On His Name

entries.title: Micah 4:6 "In that day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:6 "In that day" See note at Micah 4:1.

▣ "lame" This word means "limping flock" or "wounded sheep" (BDB 854 II). This is prophetic imagery for divine help (cf. Zeph. 3:19). It was used of Jacob in his encounter with the angel in Gen. 32:24-32.

There is obviously a parallel between v. and v. 7.

▣ "assemble" As lame and outcast are parallel, so too, the VERBS:

  1. "assemble" ‒ BDB 62, KB 74, Qal COHORTATIVE
  2. "gather" ‒ BDB 867, KB 1062, Piel COHORTATIVE

▣ "outcasts" This refers literally to sheep who have left the flock (i.e. banished ones, BDB 621, KB 673, Niphal PARTICIPLE, cf. Zeph. 3:19).

The NASB translates two different Hebrew PARTICIPLES as "outcasts"

  1. BDB 623, KB 673, Niphal PARTICIPLE, v. 6, cf. Zeph. 3:19
  2. BDB 229, KB 245, Niphal PARTICIPLE, v. 7

but #2 literally means "to be far off" (NET, Peshitta). See full note at v. 7.

▣ "Even those whom I have afflicted" YHWH Himself brought judgment on His people by the means of pagan nations (here the exiled "lame" and "outcast"; see Special Topic: The Second Coming, IV.) in order to bring them back to the place of personal faith. God disciplines those who are part of His family (cf. Heb. 12:5ff).

The Assyrians killed the weak and lame, the old and very young. Not so with YHWH, the Shepherd of Israel (cf. Ps. 23; Jesus in John 10).

entries.title: Micah 4:6-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:6-8 This continues the theme of earlier chapters in Micah, YHWH as shepherd (cf. Micah 2:12-13, Ps. 23; Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34), who cares for those who society has rejected (cf. Isa. 35:5-6; 61:1-2; Jer. 31:8; Zeph. 3:19). No one is left out or left behind!

  1. the lame (BDB 854 II, cf. Zeph. 3:19)
  2. the outcast (BDB 623, KB 673, Niphal PARTICIPLE)
  3. those far away (MT, v. 7, BDB 229, KB 245, Niphal PARTICIPLE)

Special Topic: That Day

entries.title: Micah 4:7 "a remnant. . .a strong nation"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:7 "a remnant. . .a strong nation" YHWH always starts with a small group (e.g. Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, Moses, etc.), but this small group of believers is meant to become more than the stars of heaven, the sands of the sea, and the dust of the earth (see full list as Gen. 15:5). They (believers in YHWH) are meant to fill the earth.

YHWH Himself or His Messiah will gather and accomplish this universal task (Ezek. 36:22-38). God's plan has always included all human beings (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6).

  1. in Genesis the Garden of Eden is the special place
  2. in Exodus ‒ Joshua the Promised Land is the special place
  3. in the prophets Jerusalem is the special place
  4. in the NT it is New Jerusalem coming down out of heaven (i.e. Rev. 21)

For the theological implications to "remnant" see Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses)

Special Topic: Immanuel's Person and Reign

Special Topic: YHWH's Etermal Redemptive Plan

▣
NASB, NKJV, REB  "the outcasts"
NRSV  "those who were cast off"
TEV  "those who are left"
NJB  "the far-flung"
JPSOA  "the expelled"
NIV, LXX, Peshitta  "those driven away"
NAB  "those driven off"

The Hebrew text is uncertain. Several emendations have been suggested:

  1. MT's הלא, BDB 229, KB 245, "outcasts," "those who are far off"
  2. חלה, BDB 317, "sick" (JPSOA footnote suggests Ezek. 34:4 as an example)
  3. לאה, BDB 521, "weary"

▣ "the Lord will reign over them in Mount Zion" There is a literary parallel between "reigning" and "shepherding" in the ANE (e.g. shepherd, Micah 5:4,6 and reign, Micah 4:7; 5:12).

Special Topic: Why Are OT Covenant Promises So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

Special Topic: Zion

▣ "From now on and forever" This parallels Micah 4:5d. YHWH's promises are sure. God's plans are permanent. However,

  1. There is a progressive revelation; the OT has been fulfilled by the NT (i.e. Matt. 5:17-19).
  2. Unconditional and conditional covenants, see Special Topic: Covenant

God reveals Himself in fuller ways and categories, but the goal is always life with Him!

For the concept of "forever," see Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios)

entries.title: Micah 4:8 "tower of the flock"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:8 "tower of the flock" This is possibly

  1. a special place name near Bethlehem itself, where sacrificial sheep for daily sacrifice were raised (i.e. Jerome and possibly Gen. 35:21 or Migdal-eder, JPSOA). This will become the focus of prophecy in Micah 5:2 (cf. Luke 2:8-20), which relates to the Messiah's (who is the sinless Lamb of God, cf. John 1:29) birthplace where the daily lambs for sacrifice (i.e. the Continual) are kept year round by Levitical shepherds.
  2. it refers to the king/shepherd watching over his people from the capital (here it is God or His Messiah). See Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

It is possible, using poetic synonymous parallelism, to understand several phrases:

  1. "in Mount Zion," Micah 4:7 line 3
  2. "tower of the flock," Micah 4:8 line 1
  3. "hill of the daughter of Zion," Micah 4:8, line 2 (cf. Micah 4:10,13)
  4. "the daughter of Jerusalem," Micah 4:8 line 5

as all referring to the capital of Judah (i.e. Jerusalem, cf. Isa. 24:23).

▣ "Hill of the daughter of Zion" This is possibly another place name, Ophel (BDB 779 I). Ophel was the district of Jerusalem where David's palace was located. It may be an allusion to a restored Davidic dynasty (cf. 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17).

For more information of "daughter of . . ." see notes at Amos 5:2 and Jer. 46:11.

▣ "Even the former dominion will come" This section may reflect Isa. 1:24-26. After Judah is judged, she will be restored to her previous greatness. This, of course, is imagery for restoration because, in reality, her future is far more extensive (i.e. universal, cf. Micah 5:4; Ps. 2:8; 22:27-28; 59:13; 72:8) than her past (i.e. kingdom of David and Solomon).

entries.title: Micah 4:9-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:9-13 The historical setting is again ambiguous, but because of Micah 4:10, it seems to reflect the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. by Neo-Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II.

Special Topic: Kings of Neo-Babylon

entries.title: Micah 4:9 "why do you cry out so loudly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:9 "why do you cry out so loudly" This refers to the time of exile (see Jer. 8:19). The "you" is FEMININE SINGULAR and refers to Jerusalem or Judah.

▣ "Is there no king among you" This seems to be a sarcastic comment on chapter 3. The king was God's representative, and yet, if the king is evil, to whom can the people turn?

▣ "has your counselor perished" King and counselor are parallel and refer to the head of the royal line. In Isa. 9:6 it is one of several titles of the coming Messianic king (see Isa. 3:1-3). Here it relates back to the false religious leaders of Micah 3:5-7.

Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

▣ "like a woman in childbirth" Birthing (cf. Micah 4:10 lines 1-3) is OT imagery for judgment and pain (cf. Isa. 42:14; Jer. 4:31; 6:24). In Mark 13:8 and Rom. 8:22 it is used of the birth pangs of the New Age (i.e. for ever and ever).

Special Topic: Birth Pains

4:10
NASB, Peshitta  "Writhe and labor to bring forth"
NKJV  "be in pain and labor to bring forth"
NRSV  "writhe and groan"
TEV  "twist and groan"
NJB  "writhe in pain and cry aloud"
LXX  "suffer pain, be courageous"
JPSOA  "writhe and scream"

Both of these VERBS ("writhe" BDB 296, KB 297, and "labor," lit. "burst forth," BDB 161, KB 189) are Qal IMPERATIVES.

▣ "For now you will go out of the city, Dwell in the field" This is specifically referring to a forced exile after the capture of Jerusalem. These people will be forced to live out of doors while they are being marched to new homes and fields far away in Babylon.

▣ "And go to Babylon" This is a specific allusion to the powerful Mesopotamian nation that conquered Assyria and the Fertile Crescent. Assyria took captive the Northern Ten Tribes (Israel) in 722 B.C. (cf. chapters 1-2). Neo-Babylon took captive the southern tribes (Judah) in 586 B B.C. (cf. Micah 3:12).

Many scholars are surprised at such a specific reference to Neo-Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs. 20:18). This same non-chronological aspect can be seen in Isaiah 13-14. However, it must also be mentioned that Babylon can be a general way of referring to Mesopotamia, for there was a Babylonian Empire before Assyria (i.e. Old Babylon) and even long before that (cf. Gen. 10:10).

It could also be imagery, following Gen. 11:4-9, referring to anti-God world powers (like Daniel 2; 7; 8). This would follow John the Apostle's use in the book of the Revelation (cf. Rev. 14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2,10,21).

▣  "There you will be rescued;

There the Lord will redeem you

From the hand of your enemies" Here is another glimpse of hope (lines 7-9) amidst the blackness of judgment (lines 1-6). There is another radical subject break after Micah 4:10. The new subject is introduced in Micah 4:11-12. The text moves from deliverance to another future attack beyond their return from Babylon (i.e. Dan. 9:24-27; Ezekiel 38-39). I think it refers to the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by Rome in A.D. 70. See my exegetical notes free online involving Jesus' Olivet Discourse, Paul's "Man of Lawlessness," and John's book of Revelation.

Special Topic: Ransom/Redeem

▣ "From the hand of your enemies" "Hand" was an idiom for power.

Special Topic: Hand

entries.title: Micah 4:11 "now many nations have been assembled against you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:11 "now many nations have been assembled against you" This seems to refer to the mercenary troops found both in the Assyrian (e.g. Sennacherib, 701 B.C.) and Neo-Babylonian armies (e.g. Nebuchadnezzar, 586 B.C.). One example of these mercenaries is Edom, specifically stated in Obadiah.

However, those who are looking for a certain pre-millennial position often find credence in their position from passages like this in the Prophets.

Special Topic: The Second Coming (chart)

▣
NASB  "Let her be polluted"
NKJV, Peshitta  "Let her be defiled"
NRSV  "Let her be profaned"
TEV  "must be destroyed"
NJB  "Let us desecrate her"
REB  "Let her suffer outrage"

The VERB (BDB 337, KB 335, Qal IMPERFECT, but JUSSIVE in meaning) means "to be polluted or profaned" (cf. Ps. 106:38; Jer. 3:1,9). This same root is used in Isa. 9:16; 10:6).

▣
NASB, NJB  "let our eyes gloat over Zion"
NKJV, Peshitta  "let our eyes look upon"
JPSOA  "let our eye obscenely gaze on Zion"
NRSV  "let our eyes gaze upon"
TEV  "we will see"
REB  "let us gloat over Zion"
LXX  "our eyes shall behold Zion"

The VERB is parallel to the one above. There (BDB 302, 301, Qal JUSSIVE) is one general term "to see."

 The USB Translator's Handbook suggests that these two VERBS had a sexual connotation and this was the reason why

  1. the imagery of "daughter" is used in Micah 4:8, 10, 13 (p. 129)
  2. possibly the Promised Land's ritual defilement by foreign troops is the connotation of the two parallel VERBS (p. 129)

entries.title: Micah 4:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:12 When those who do not know YHWH or His Word view history, they see Him judging His own people. They miss the goal of a special covenant people as a means for all people to know God. Abraham's descendants did not keep the covenant, did not reveal God, so God chose to reveal Himself (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

In this chapter the tension between believing nations vs. attacking, unbelieving nations is accentuated. The poetry is brief and ambiguous. It is difficult (impossible) to systematize it. These are flashes of truth, of future events, or literary imagery. Three great truths are taught:

  1. YHWH's will of a restored believing humanity will be a reality.
  2. Some will not believe and will attack God by attacking His people.
  3. One group will be with God forever; one group will be destroyed (possibly origin of v. 5)!

▣ "He has gathered them" This seems to imply that God has gathered Israel's and Judah's enemies to allow her to destroy them (cf. Micah 4:13; Isaiah 13-14; Ezekiel 38-39; Joel 4; Zechariah 14).

entries.title: Micah 4:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:13 Verses 12-13 must be taken together to understand YHWH's comment. He calls His restored covenant people to devastate those pagan nations which He used to punish His own people for their sins (cf. Micah 4:12; Isa. 41:15-16; Jer. 51:20-23; Habakkuk).

The first two VERBS ("arise" BDB 877, KB 1086 and "thresh" BDB 190, KB 218) are both Qal IMPERATIVES.

But in Micah 4:13 YHWH is speaking to His restored covenant people (i.e. New Covenant, cf. Jer. 31:31-34). One day His people will be victorious. God wanted to use Abraham's descendants. He wanted the world to know Him and come to Him, but Abraham's seed did not and the world could not!

▣  "That you may devote. . .their unjust gain

And their wealth to the Lord" This is imagery taken from "holy war" (i.e. Jericho). YHWH's people avenging themselves on the very nations that devastated her by YHWH's help was seen as the nations' wealth being given to YHWH because it is "holy" (i.e. herem).

Special Topic: Curse

▣ "to the Lord of all the earth" Again, notice this universal emphasis. In context this chapter relates to YHWH's first covenant people, but in light of Jesus, it refers to the New Covenant people!

The doctrines of YHWH as Creator and the assertion of monotheism demands a worldwide emphasis!

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why are the books of Isaiah and Micah so similar?
  2. Is it unusual for the Old Testament prophecies to have a universal implication?
  3. Why is Micah 4:5 out of context?
