READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Micah contains many very specific prophecies. See Introduction III. Genre, D. These prophecies demonstrate the unique character of Hebrew scripture.
    Special Topic: Inspiration

  2. Some translations take Micah 5:1 (i.e. Micah 4:14 in Hebrew text) with Micah 4 (cf. TEV). If so then it relates to Micah 4:9-11a, where Jerusalem is attacked and exiled.
     However, other translations take it with Micah 5:1-5a (NASB, NJB, NIV), which would form a contrast between
    1. Jerusalem with its faithless king and evil leaders
    2. Bethlehem with a great coming king and godly leader

  3. This chapter is very specific about the birthplace of the Messiah. Micah wrote in the eighth century B.C. and precisely predicted the village of Jesus' birth. Some will deny the date of Micah, but if you do not accept the 750's then Micah was translated into Greek (i.e. the Septuagint in 250-150 B.C.; see Special Topic: Septuagint). This is still well over a hundred fifty years before His birth.
     The predictive element unique to the Bible shows:
    1. the inspiration of the Bible
    2. the sovereignty of YHWH over history
    3. the reality of the Messiahship of Jesus of Nazareth (Special Topic: The Bble (its uniqueness and inspiration)

      The Jewish leaders were asked by Herod the Great where the Messiah was to be born (cf. Matt. 2) and they knew exactly the answer (Micah 5)!

  4. This chapter also hints at the pre-existence (see note at Micah 5:2, lines 4,5) of the Messiah as well as the type of reign He will employ (Micah 5:4-5). This is shockingly specific prophecy. What a wonderful and accurate Bible we have been given by God.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

5:1
NASB  "Now muster yourselves in troops, daughter of troops"
NKJV  "now gather yourself in troops, O daughter of troops"
NRSV  "now you are walled around with a wall"
TEV  "People of Jerusalem, gather your forces"
NJB  "now look to your fortifications, fortress"
Peshitta  "now you shall go forth in a raid"
 O daughter of mighty maidens"

This verse is Micah 4:14 in the Hebrew text. There are several translation options:

  1. The NASB, NKJV, and TEV follow the MT, "gather" (BDB 151 I, cf. Jer. 5:7).
  2. The Septuagint has "now you are walled about with a wall" (i.e. siege, cf. NRSV, REB). It changes the Hebrew VERB "gather" (BDB 151, KB 177, Hithpoel IMPERFECT) to a similar Hebrew word meaning "to build a wall" (BDB 154, i.e. strengthen against a siege, cf. Ezek. 13:5, NJB).
  3. Another possible translation is "you are slashing yourself, daughter of slashes" (BDB 151, but it would require a revocalization, cf. JPSOA, Moffatt translation, NET). This last possibility could be accurate because of the connection between "slashing oneself" and
    1. idolatry (cf. Lev. 19:28; 21:5; Deut. 14:1; 1 Kgs. 18:28; Jer. 47:5; Hosea 7:14) or
    2. grief (cf. Deut. 14:1; Jer. 16:6; 41:5; 47:5; 48:37)

The UBS Text Project, p. 319, gives "gash yourself, daughter of a band" a "B" rating.

Verse 1 describes the situation as it was (Jerusalem about to be sieged), where Micah 5:2-5 describes the situation that will be in the end time (Jerusalem home of the great King). This same temporal transition can be seen in Micah 5:5-9 in contrast with Micah 5:10-14.

Chapter 4, Micah 5:9-13, deals with Jerusalem. It is possible that 5:1 (MT 4:14) is one paragraph relating to a besieged capital (Jerusalem). See Contextual Insights, B.

If Micah 5:1 goes with 5:2-5a, then there is a contrast between weak, helpless Jerusalem and YHWH's new leader from Bethlehem (David's hometown). The Judean monarchy is hopelessly lost in sin and faithlessness (except for a few godly kings, e.g. Hezekiah, Josiah). YHWH will raise up another faithful king of David's line, who will fully follow Him (cf. Gen. 49:9-10; 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17:1)!

▣ "They have laid siege against us" The VERB (BDB 962, KB 1321) is a Qal PERFECT. Remember the time setting is not in the VERB, but in the context. This obviously refers to a siege, but which one? There are several theories.

  1. The historical setting may be Sennacherib's invasion of Judah and his unsuccessful siege of Jerusalem in 701 B.C. ( cf. 2 Kgs. 19:35-36).
  2. Nebechadnezzar II also invaded and besieged Jerusalem in 586 B.C. (cf. 2 Kgs. 24-25).
  3. Many scholars believe this may also reflect the future invasion of Jerusalem and destruction of the temple by Titus in A.D. 70 (cf. Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 21); please see my new notes on the Olivet Discourse and the book of Revelation (2024) online.

Number 1 fits the author's time best, while #3 fits the Messiah's time best.

▣ "With a rod" The term "rod" (BDB 986) meant a stripped tree branch (shorter than a staff) used as a means of discipline

  1. for children, Prov. 10:13; 13:24; 22:8,15; 23:13,14; 26:3; 29:15
  2. as imagery for YHWH's judgment on the nations, Ps. 2:9 (cf. 110:5-6); Isa. 9:4; Rev. 2:27; 19:15
  3. as imagery for judgment on His own people, Isa. 10:5,24; 14:29

Assyria was called the "rod of God's anger" in Isa. 10:5,24. However, God will also strike Assyria because of her sins (cf. Isa. 30:31).

"Rod" is also a Hebrew idiom for a king ruling (BDB 986, cf. Micah 7:14; Rev. 2:27; 12:5; 19:15).

▣ "they will smite the judge of Israel on the cheek" "The judge" is a title for the King of Judah, here called "Israel." To smite one on the cheek was a sign of great insult (cf. 1 Kgs. 22:24; Job 16:10; Lam. 3:30; Acts 23:2), which shows Babylon's contempt and Judah's weakness.

Rotherham's Emphasized Bible asserts that this judge is the Messiah (p. 887), which assumes Micah 5:1 goes with chapter 5, not chapter 4.

entries.title: Micah 5:2 "Bethlehem Ephrathah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:2 "Bethlehem Ephrathah" Ephrathah (i.e. a clan of the tribe of Judah, cf 1 Sam. 17:12; Ruth 1:2; 4:11; also note 1 Chr. 2:19,24,50) is added because there was another "house of bread" (Beth-lehem) in the northern tribal allocation of Zebulun (cf. Josh. 19:15). Bethlehem was known as Ephrath (cf. Gen. 35:19; 48:7; Ruth 4:11). It was a very small village, only noted because it was the birthplace of King David (cf. 1 Sam. 16:1, and thereby, a way to refer to a future Davidic Messianic King, cf. 2 Samuel 7; Psalm 89). This verse is quoted in Matt. 2:6 and alluded to in Luke 2:4 and John 7:42.

▣ little" This term (BDB 859 I ) is often used in a pejorative sense of least.

  1. clans, 1 Sam. 9:21
  2. tribes, Ps. 68:27
  3. horns, Dan. 8:9
  4. towns, Micah 5:2

(list from NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 830)

▣ "clans" The term "clans" is the Hebrew term "thousands" (BDB 48 II). The Hebrew term for thousand, eleph, can be used as:

  1. a family or clan unit, Num. 10:4; Josh. 22:14; Jdg. 6:15; 1 Sam. 10:19; 23:23; Micah 5:2; Zech. 9:7
  2. a military unit, Exod. 18:21,25; Deut. 1:15
  3. a literal thousand, Gen. 20:16; Exod. 32:28
  4. a symbol, Gen. 24:60; Exod. 20:6 (Deut. 7:9); 34:7; Jer. 32:18

Bethlehem was so small that she is not even mentioned in Joshua 15 as supplying troops for the Judean army, or in Nehemiah 11 as supplying workers for rebuilding Jerusalem's walls.

Special Topic: Thousand (eleph)

▣ "of Judah" Because of Moses' prediction about the descendants of Jacob's son, Judah (BDB 397) in Gen. 49:8-12, esp. v. 10, it became the accepted prophecy that the Messiah would be of Judah's line, family of Jesse (cf. 2 Samuel 7).

▣ "for Me" This phrase is emphasized in the MT. The Messiah comes at YHWH's bidding. He is YHWH's full and perfect, human, righteous leader, One who accurately and completely reflects and reveals the God of Israel. The students of the OT (the rabbis) were not expecting an incarnation (i.e. God becoming a man), but an empowerment (i.e. like the Judges). God Himself was the true king (cf. 1 Sam. 8:7).

▣
NASB  "His goings forth are from long ago,
 From the days of eternity"
NKJV  "Whose goings forth have been from of old.
 From everlasting"
NRSV  "Whose origin is from of old
 From ancient days"
TEV  "Whose family line goes back to ancient time"
NJB, REB  "Whose origins go back to the distant past,
 To the days of old"
JPSOA  "One whose origin is from old,
 From ancient times"
Peshitta  "Whose origins go back to the distant past,
 Whose goings forth have been predicted from of old,
  from eternity"

These two lines are parallel. The VERB, "going forth" (BDB 422, KB 425, Qal IMPERATIVE) is a very common VERB. It was used in Micah eight times.

  1. of the Lord coming in Micah 1:3
  2. of YHWH's law going forth in Micah 4:2
  3. of repentant Israel being restored in Micah 7:9 (a new exodus, 7:15)

It can refer to the Messiah's origin (NRSV, NJB) or actions (cf. Micah 5:4 and 5a).

These two lines could refer to

  1. the pre-existence of the Messiah (i.e. as "Wisdom," Prov. 8:22-31 or "the Angel of the Lord" (see Special Topic: Angel of the Lord); for pre-existence, cf. John 1:1,14-15; 8:56-59; 16:28; 17:5; 1 Cor. 8:9; Phil. 2:6-7; Col. 1:17; Heb. 1:3; 10:5-7)
  2. a way of referring to famous descendants of the past (i.e. Abraham, Noah, or more probably, David, cf. Micah 7:14,20; Amos 9:11).

This whole verse alludes to a Davidic king, of David's line, from David's hometown. David was viewed as the ideal king (cf. 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17). This means that in this specific context, this phrase could refer back to David's day.

The term "eternity" (BDB 761) is 'olam, which must be interpreted in context. See Special Topic: Forever ('olam and aiōnios).

The NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 347, which discusses 'olam, makes this comment,

"While it is tempting to see here a reference to the eternal preexistence of the Messiah, no such an idea is found in biblical or postbiblical Jewish literature before the 'Similitudes of Enoch' (first century B.C. ‒ first century A.D.; see I Enoch 48:2-6."

I think, although there are hints in the OT of an incarnation, the Jewish leaders of Jesus' day were surprised at His claims of equality with YHWH (e.g. Mark 2:5-7; John 1:1-14; 8:58 and Paul, 2 Cor. 4:4; Col. 1:15; Phil. 2:6; Titus 2:13). The NT authors see this verse as relating to Jesus' birth (i.e. Matt. 2:6; John 7:42).

A partial list of OT texts that have been used to assert the full Deity of Jesus follows:

  1. Ps. 2:7, quoted in Heb. 1:5 (see esp. 1:2-3)
  2. Ps. 45:6-7 quoted in Heb. 1:8-9
  3. Ps. 110:1 quoted in Heb. 1:13
  4. Isa. 9:6; Jer. 23:5-6; Micah 5:2 alluded to in Luke 1:32
  5. Dan. 7:13 quoted in Matt. 26:64; Mark14:62
  6. Zech. 13:7 quoted in Matt. 26:31; Mark 14:27
  7. Mal. 3:1 quoted in Mark 1:1-3; Luke 2:26-27

Special Topic: The Trinity

Special Topic: The Bible (its uniqueness and inspiration)

entries.title: Micah 5:2-5a
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:2-5a This whole paragraph marks a radical transition from God's judgment (siege, exile) on Jerusalem and Judah to God's marvelous restoration (cf. Micah 4:6-8,12-13; 7:18-20). This vacillation is common in prophetic literature and perhaps is

  1. the work of later editors
  2. the mind set (antithetical parallelism) of the Hebrew prophets

Special Topic: Eastern Literature (biblical paradoxes)

entries.title: Micah 5:3 "He will give them up until the time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:3 "He will give them up until the time" In context the PRONOUN can refer to

  1. YHWH
  2. His Messiah

It think it refers to

  1. YHWH in Micah 5:3, line 1
  2. but to the Messiah in Micah 5:3, line 3
  3. is purposeful ambiguity!

The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT) is another very common VERB, which can mean "give," "put," or "set." Here it connotes "deliver up," usually in a judgment context (cf. Num. 21:3; Jdg. 20:13; 1 Sam. 11:12; 2 Sam. 14:7; 20:21; 1 Kgs. 14:16; Hosea 11:8).

▣ "she who is in labor has borne a child" There are several possible biblical antecedents:

  1. It goes back to YHWH's first promise of redemption by a male deliverer through a woman in Gen. 3:15; see Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan.
  2. It relates to Micah's contemporary, Isaiah, who several years earlier mentioned a special birth (cf. Isa. 7:14; 9:6; 11:1-16).
  3. It goes back to Micah 4:9-10, which uses the same imagery for Jerusalem's seige and exile, see Special Topic: Birth Pains.
  4. It relates to the Messianic community (i.e. the faithful remnant; see Special Topic: The Remnant), as in Revelation 12, bringing forth the Messiah.

The whole point of Micah 5:3 is that God has allowed a limited judgment to overwhelm His faithless covenant people in order to gloriously restore them (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36; Jer. 31:31-34); Micah 4:1-4; 7:18-20.

▣  "Then the remainder of His brethren

Will return to the sons of Israel" These two lines of poetry may refer to one or two groups:

  1. "the remnant" (see Special Topic: The Remnant [three senses])
  2. "the sons of Israel"
    1. referring to the northern ten tribes (cf. Isa. 10:26-27)
    2. referring to Judah by the collective title (see Special Topic: Israel [the name])

Historically this would mostly refer to the Judeans taken into exile reuniting with those who remained in the Promised Land, but eschatologically it refers to "all Israel" (cf. Romans 9-11, esp. 9:6; John 10:16). The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 7, p. 428, says it refers to "brothers" of the coming ruler (cf. Micah 5:2). As always, poetic prophecy is brief, ambiguous, and difficult to interpret. It is almost impossible to interpret without

  1. a specific historical setting
  2. a literary context
  3. OT or NT parallel passages

See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic (this has been a very helpful book for me in interpreting prophecy).

Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry

Special Topic: Prophecy (OT)

▣ "return" There is a play on the word shub (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERFECT), which denotes

  1. a literal physical returning (from exile)
  2. a spiritual repentance (from idolatry and rebellion)

This alludes to Micah 2:12-13 and 4:6-8.

Special Topic: Repentance (OT)

entries.title: Micah 5:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:4 This is a description of the characteristics of the Messianic reign (cf. Isa. 9:6-7; 11:1-5,6-9,11-16):

  1. He will stand (i.e. endure or remain, e.g. Ps. 102:26; 111:3,10; 112:3,9; Eccl. 1:4; Isa. 14:26; 66:22; Hag. 2:5)
  2. He will shepherd His people (David was a shepherd, YHWH is described by him in these terms in Psalm 23, typical ANE imagery for a king)
  3. He will come in the strength of the Lord
  4. He will come in the majesty of the name of the Lord, his God
  5. He will be great
  6. He will reign to the ends of the earth (BDB 75 e.g. Ps. 2:8; 22:27-28; 59:13; 72:8; see Special Topic: Land, Country, Earth)
  7. In Micah 5:5, line 1 (which should go with Micah 5:4) He will reign in peace (cf. Micah 5:4, line 4; see Special Topic: Peace (OT))

Notice how Micah 5:4 describes the same time period as Micah 4:1-4.

Special Topic: Messianic Era

entries.title: Micah 5:5a "And this One will be our peace"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:5a "And this One will be our peace" Peace is the Hebrew word shalom (BDB 1022). It speaks of wholeness. Jews today use it for a greeting and a farewell. Its eschatological use here is possibly a contrast to the contemporary false prophets' message of peace (cf. Micah 3:5 and 5:5, line 2, Micah 5:6).

This verse is speaking of a ruler who will bring peace (cf. Micah 5:4) and will himself be called peace (cf. Isa. 9:6; Eph. 2:14).

Special Topic: Peace (OT, shalom)

entries.title: Micah 5:5 line 2b-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:5 line 2b-9 Assyria was YHWH's chosen instrument to punish Israel (cf. Isa. 10:5). His covenant people had gone so far into Ba'al worship they did not know Him (cf. Hosea 11:1-4). He breaks His covenant so He can reestablish it (i.e. New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34, described in Ezek. 36:22-36)! Assyria was a limited judgment (cf. Micah 5:3).

The time frame for this paragraph is uncertain. Assyria may be a way of referring to

  1. all godly anti-YHWH nations (cf. Zech. 10:10-11), which would be similar to the name Babylon (used in the book of Revelation)
  2. purposeful ambiguity by specifically mentioning "Babylon" in Micah 4:10 and "Assyria" here.

Special Topic: Kings of Assyria

Special Topic: Kings of Neo-Babylon

entries.title: Micah 5:5 "Then we will raise against him
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:5 "Then we will raise against him

Seven shepherds and eight leaders of men" Number sequences are common in

  1. Ugaritic
  2. OT literature (e.g. Prov. 6:16; 30:15,18,21,29; Amos 1:3,6,9,11,13; 2:1,4,6)
  3. Ecclesiasticus 11:25

The emphasis is on the adequate number of godly leaders to accomplish YHWH's will who will be available in that day. Assyria will be judged by Him in the end (cf. Isa. 10:24-27).

There is the question of why does the text have "we will raise" (BDB 877, KB 1086, Hiphil PERFECT with waw). Does this imply that scattered Israel will be the source of God's deliverance or is it a way of referring to God's actions (cf.v. 3 line 1) or His Messiah (cf. Micah 5:3 line 3; Micah 5:4-5 line 1)? This same tension is seen when comparing, "we will raise," Micah 5:5 line 4 and "they will shepherd," Micah 5:6 line 1 vs. "he will deliver" (BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil PERFECT with waw). Micah 5:6 line 3.

The ambiguity of this text and the lack of any historical basis for Jewish soldiers conquering Assyria cause many (and rightly so) to

  1. make Assyria stand for any world power who is against God's people
  2. the conqueror is not "they" but "he" (the ideal ruler of Micah 5:2-5a) will subdue all end-time opposition (similar to Psalm 2 or Ezekiel 38-39 or Daniel 11:36-45)

entries.title: Micah 5:6 "Nimrod"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:6 "Nimrod" This name (BDB 650) relates to the founding of Babel (i.e. Babylon) and Nineveh (i.e. Assyria in Gen. 10:8-12). Nimrod is called a mighty hunter who established the first kingdom of Mesopotamia ("the land between the Rivers," i.e. the Tigris and Euphrates). Therefore, these two terms, Assyria and Nimrod, are

  1. simply SYNONYMS
  2. it refers to neo-Babylon under Nebopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II
▣
NASB, NKJV  "at its entrances"
NRSV, REB, NET  "with a drawn sword"
NJB  "with naked blade"
JPSOA  "in its gates"
LXX  "with her ditch"
Peshitta  "with their anger"

The MT is reflected by the NASB. JPSOA footnote suggests an emendation to "with drawn blades" and suggests Ps. 37:14; 55:22 as corroborating texts.

  1. MT ‒ בפתחיה
  2. emendation ‒ בפתימה

The UBS Text Project, p. 321, gives the emendation a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "He will deliver us from the Assyrian when he attacks our land" This is not what happened in history! Therefore, is this

  1. a future reference to Cyrus II (i.e. 539 B.C. the city of Babylon falls, cf. Isa. 44-45)
  2. a reference to the eschatological future (i.e. Messianic period; see Special Topic: Messianic Era)
  3. a reference to the message of the contemporary false prophets (more probable)

entries.title: Micah 5:7 "dew from the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:7 "dew from the Lord" "Dew" in the OT has several meanings:

  1. God's blessing, Gen. 27:28; Num. 11:9; Deut. 33:13,28; Prov. 19:12; Hosea 14:5; Zech. 8:12
  2. lack of it was a divine curse, 2 Sam. 1:21; 1 Kgs. 17:1; Hag. 1:10
  3. it evaporated quickly in the sunlight, so it was imagery for transient things, Exod. 16:13-14; Isa. 18:4; Hosea 6:4; 13:3 (similar to mist, vapor, smoke)
  4. imagery for life or youth, Isa. 26:19
  5. imagery of pervasiveness, 2 Sam. 17:12

(see Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, pp. 206-207)

▣
NASB  "do not wait for man"
NKJV, Peshitta  "that tarry for no man"
NRSV  "which do not depend upon people"
TEV  "They will depend on God, not people"
NJB  "which do not depend on human agency"
REB  "which does not wait for mortal command"
JPSOA  "which do not look to any man"
LXX  "that none among sons of man may assemble
 or resist"

This VERB (BDB 875 I, KB 1082, Piel IMPERFECT) in the Piel form has three basic meanings:

  1. look eagerly for, Job 3:9; 6:19; Isa. 5:2,4,7; 59:9,11; Jer. 8:15; 13:16; 14:19,22; Hosea 12:6
  2. lie in wait for, Ps. 56:6; 119:95
  3. wait (linger) for, Micah 5:7

Humans wait patiently for moisture because they can do nothing to provide it. It must come "from the Lord."

▣
NASB  "delay"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "wait for"
REB  "linger"

This VERB (BDB 403, KB 407, Piel IMPERFECT) in Piel form has two meanings:

  1. wait for (Piel, BDB #1)
  2. hope for (Piel, BDB #2)

Humans know that there is that part of life (i.e. spiritual vitality) which they cannot produce, manufacture, or implement themselves!

entries.title: Micah 5:7-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:7-9 Quite often in Micah (and other prophets) there has been the promise that YHWH would bring His remnant (see Special Topic: The Remnant (three senses) back to Jerusalem. However, in this context, He will scatter the remnant of faithful believers throughout the earth that they might

  1. be a blessing (i.e. "dew from the Lord"), Micah 5:7
  2. be a champion for justice and godliness, Micah 5:8

If this is accurate then YHWH is using the exiles to scatter His people. His scattered people are His witnesses to all the nations, which fulfills Gen. 12:2-3; 22:18; 26:4; Acts 3:25; Gal. 3:8!

However, I must admit that it is possible to see both phrases (i.e. Micah 5:7-8) relating to judgment (cf. Micah 5:9; 2 Sam. 17:12). There is much discussion as to whom this verse refers. Some see it as scattered Israel, some see it as the end-time people of God (cf. Romans 9-11; 2:28-29; Galatians 3).

It is just possible that this entire context (i.e. 5b-9) reflects the false hopes and predictions of the false prophets (cf. Micah 3:5). Micah is characterized by radical switching from judgment to redemption. If so, then Micah 5:1-5a is the true prophet's prediction, while Micah 5:5b-9 relates to false hope of the false prophets!

Special Topic: Why Do OT Covenant Promises Seem So Different from NT Covenant Promises?

Special Topic: YHWH'S Eternal Redemptive Plan

entries.title: Micah 5:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:8 It is obvious that Micah 5:7 and 8 are parallel in structure. The interpretive issue is, are they parallel in emphasis? Verse 7 seems to be a positive emphasis, but Micah 5:8 seems negative (cf. Micah 5:9).

They may be another example of antithetical parallelism (e.g. Prov. 19:12 uses both "lion" and "dew"). Dispersed Israel will be both a blessing and a curse. YHWH will bring truth to the nations through them, but also judgment. Light brings responsibility (cf. Luke 12:48).

▣ "lion" Lion is common imagery for strength and power in the ancient Near East.

Special Topic: Lions in the OT

▣ "there is none to rescue" This is an idiom of divine power (cf. Deut. 32:39; Job 10:7; Ps. 50:22; Hosea 5:14 and related phrases in Job 9:12; 23:13; and Isa. 42:44).

entries.title: Micah 5:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:9 This strophe in verses Micah 5:7-9 is so ambiguous that several theories have been put forth by translators and commentators. Micah 5:9 may be a clear summary of verses Micah 5:7-8, addressed directly to the conquering eschatological remnant.

The term "cut off" (BDB 503, KB 500, Niphal IMPERFECT, possibly in JUSSIVE sense) seems to foreshadow Micah 5:10,11,12,13, which is an obvious judgment context related to Canaanite societies which trusted in

  1. its military
  2. its fortifications
  3. its religious practices and idols

This false hope and false worship affected many nations in and around Canaan (cf. Gen. 15:16), including Israel and Judah.

entries.title: Micah 5:10 "in that day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:10 "in that day" This is a reference to God's judgment day (see note at Micah 4:1, 6).

Special Topic: That Day

▣
NASB, NKJV  "cut off"
NRSV, JPSOA, Peshitta  "destroy"
TEV  "take away"
NJB  "tear. . .tear away"
REB  "slaughter"
LXX  "utterly destroy"

The VERB (BDB 503, KB 500, Hiphil PERFECT with waw) in the Hiphil form is common imagery ("cut off") for a complete destruction and removal (e.g. Micah 5:9,10,11,12,13; Isa. 9:14; 10:7; 14:22; Amos 1:5,8; 2:3; Zech. 9:10).

▣ "your horses" YHWH's people (i.e. kings), against the direct commands from Him (cf. Deut. 17:16), went to Egypt to multiply their military power (i.e. chariots). This need not be literal, but stands for a reliance on military power instead of God (cf. Zech. 9:10), in every age!

▣ "chariots" Chariots were the ultimate weapon of that day. They seem to have been introduced into this area (originally from the Hyksos rulers in Egypt) by the Phoenicians or Philistines who plated them with iron and made them the most formidable weapon available (at least on flat ground).

Special Topic: Chariots

entries.title: Micah 5:10-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:10-15 YHWH's people were trusting not in Him, but

  1. in their military might, Micah 5:10
  2. in their fortifications, Micah 5:11
  3. their sorceries, Micah 5:12
  4. their idolatry, Micah 5:13-14 (e.g. Isa. 2:8)

YHWH must stop this by asserting His power and will. This repeated use of "I" reminds me of Ezek. 36:22-36 (description of the New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34).

entries.title: Micah 5:11 "And tear down all your fortifications"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:11 "And tear down all your fortifications" We know from Assyrian documents that in 701 B.C. Sennacherib captured forty six walled cities of Judah (cf. Micah 5:14b).

entries.title: Micah 5:12 "sorceries. . .fortune tellers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:12 "sorceries. . .fortune tellers" Micah 5:12-14 refers to the activity of sorcerers (BDB 506, KB 503, attempting to know and control the future) among the people of God. They are condemned in Lev. 19:26 and Deut. 18:9-22. See full note in Deuteronomy 18. Many were brought into Israel by Jezebel (cf. 2 Kgs. 9:22).

Special Topic: Magic

▣ "from your hand" This may refer to bracelets, amulets worn by followers. NET Bible has "magic charms." But, the LXX and Peshitta see the phrase as imagery for "among you" or "in your midst."

entries.title: Micah 5:13 "carved images. . .sacred pillars. . .the work of your hands"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:13 "carved images. . .sacred pillars. . .the work of your hands" These refer to various idols which the people of God were worshiping (cf. Gen. 28:18,22; Deut. 16:22).

Special Topic: Idolatry

5:14
NASB  "Asherim"
NKJV  "wooden images"
NRSV, NJB, REB  "sacred poles"
TEV  "the images of the goddess Asherah"
JPSOA  "sacred pillars"
LXX  "steles"
Peshitta  "groves"

This refers to some type of wooden pole (BDB 81, i.e. carved stake or live tree representing the tree of life) positioned next to the uplifted rock on Ba'al platforms (i.e. heights). It represented the female fertility god of Canaan (e.g. Deut. 7:5; 12:3; 16:21; Jdg. 3:7; 6:25,26; 1 Kgs. 14:23; 2 Kgs. 17:10; 18:4; 2 Chr. 31:1), while the sacred pillars of Micah 5:13 refer to the male fertility god (i.e. Ba'al). These foreign fertility gods and goddesses were introduced from Phoenicia (Jezebel) and were very popular among the people of God (cf 1 Kings 18-19).

Special Topic: Asherim

▣
NASB, NKJV, TEV, REB, Peshitta, LXX  "your cities"
NRSV  "your towns"

Some scholars speculate that since "cities" were referred to earlier (i.e. Micah 5:11, BDB 746) and that the same root here should be paralleled to "Asherim" of Micah 5:14 line 1. To do so they have speculated a Ugaritic root or possibly an Arabic root (cf. REB, "blood-spattered altars").

The Jewish Study Bible's footnote, Rotherham's footnote, and the NET Bible suggest an emendation which yields "idols."

  1. "your cities" ‒ עריך
  2. "your images" ‒ צריך
  3. "your idols" ‒ עצביך

entries.title: Micah 5:15 "I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:15 "I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath" The terms (plus PREPOSITION "in") "anger" (BDB 60 I) and "wrath" (BDB 404) are hendiays which intensify the meaning (i.e. in great wrath).

Another option is to see Micah 5:15 as a separate thought. YHWH will purify and restore His covenant exiled people, but for those of the nations that do not respond (cf. Micah 5:7) He will destroy all idolaters.

▣ "On the nations which have not obeyed" The VERB (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal PERFECT) means to hear so as to obey. See note at Micah 4:1. The same term, but in an IMPERATIVE form, is repeated in Micah 6:1.

The nations who heard of YHWH from the scattered, exiled covenant people must respond to the truth they have heard (cf. Micah 5:7).

This seems to be completely out of context with the previous passage, however, it does emphasize the truth that YHWH does not play favorites with nations, even Israel and Judah. He is God of all the earth, but only the covenant people had His true word through His true prophets.

Special Topic: Listen/Hear (shema)

Special Topic: Keep

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why is it so important that Micah, who lived 750 years before the birth of Jesus, was able to pinpoint the exact location of His birth?
  2. Why are Micah 5:7-9 so unusual in the context of 8th century prophets?
  3. How is our country so like Israel in connection with Micah 5:10-14?
  4. How do you explain the similarity of Isaiah 2:6-8 with Micah 5:10-14?

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BRIEF OUTLINE OF CHAPTER 6

  1. YHWH brings His people to court in Micah 6:1-5. He documents His faithfulness to them in Micah 6:3-5. This court imagery is a common literary device in the prophets (i.e. Isa. 1; Jer. 2: Hosea 4).
    Special Topic: Prophecy (OT), IV. E.

  2. The people answer God's charges in Micah 6:6-7.

  3. The Prophet speaking for YHWH summarizes His will for His people in Micah 6:8

  4. The prophet speaking for YHWH delineates the sins of the rich and powerful of the descendants of Abraham in Micah 6:9-16. Because of them the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 are now invoked (i.e. Deut. 28:15,18,40,51). Oh my!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Micah 6:1-2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:1-2 "Hear" There are several Qal IMPERATIVES in Micah 6:1-2:

  1. "Hear" (BDB 1033, KB 1570, i.e. in the sense of a prayer petition) ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "Arise" (BDB 877, KB 1086) ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "Plead your case" (DBD 936, KB 1224) ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. "Hear" (BDB 1033, KB 1570) ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE used in a JUSSIVE sense
  5. "Listen" (BDB 1033, KB 1570) ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE

"Hear" is a way for Micah to start a new section (cf. Micah 1:1; 3:1; 6:1).

The second IMPERATIVE "arise" is MASCULINE SINGULAR. It could refer to Micah as YHWH's spokesman or collectively to the nation. Option #1 fits the context best.

This chapter is a court scene. Notice the number of terms with a legal connotation:

  1. "Arise" (i.e. to testify, i.e. Deut. 19:15-16 and false witnesses in Ps. 27:12; 35:11), Micah 6:1
  2. "Plead" (i.e. to contend in court
    1. negatively, i.e. Isa. 1:17; 3:13; 97:16
    2. positively 7:9; Ps. 103:8-14, esp. 9; Jer. 50:34)
  3. "Hear" (i.e. in the sense of a jury or judge, i.e. Micah 1:2)
  4. "Listen" (same word as #3)
  5. "Indictment" (same word as #2)
  6. "A case" (same word as #3 and #5)
  7. "Dispute" (BDB 406, KB 410, Hithpael IMPERFECT, i.e. adjudication of a judge, i.e. Isa. 2:4; Micah 4:3)

YHWH is divorcing His covenant people because of their repeated unfaithfulness (Hosea) and sin (Amos). This is the clear reality of a conditional covenant. This court scene may continue through Micah 7.

Special Topic: Listen/Hear (shema)

Special Topic: Covenant

Special Topic: YHWH's Covenant Requirements of Israel

▣ "before the mountains. . .hills" In the OT it takes two witnesses to confirm truth (cf. Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:6; 19:5). YHWH calls

  1. "the mountains" and "hills" to witness against Israel and Judah
  2. as He does "heaven and earth" (cf. Deut. 4:26; 31:28; 32:l; Ps. 50:4 and Isa. 1:2)
  3. as He does , "O peoples. . .O earth" (cf. Micah 1:2)

Several times in the OT mountains are personified (i.e. 2 Sam. 1:21; Ps. 68:15-16; Isa. 35:1). These mountains and hills were the very places (i.e. "high places") Ba'al and Asherah were worshiped.

Special Topic: Fertility Worship of the ANE

entries.title: Micah 6:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:2 This verse is legal imagery. YHWH turns from addressing His people, Judah, to address the permanent, foundational, personified witnesses, the mountains and hills.

▣ "His people" Privilege (covenant people, cf. Micah 6:3; Rom. 9:4-5) brings responsibility (cf. Luke 12:48)! This is parallel in the next line with "Israel," which is the collective designation of the covenant people.

Special Topic: Covenant

Special Topic: Israel (the name)

▣ "Even with Israel He will dispute" This does not refer to the Northern Ten Tribes (i.e. Israel) only (cf. Micah 6:16), but here to all of the tribes, the descendants of Jacob (Israel). There are consequences for covenant disobedience.

entries.title: Micah 6:3 "what have I done to you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:3 "what have I done to you" YHWh asks them to bring their complaints or charges against Him (cf. Jer. 2:5). Where, when, how has He not been faithful to His covenant responsibilities?

▣ "Answer Me" This is a legal term (BDB 772, KB 851, Qal IMPERATIVE), which means "to give evidence against" (cf. Exod. 20:16; Deut. 5:20; 2 Sam. 1:16). YHWH is acting as one party in a divorce case.

entries.title: Micah 6:3-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:3-5 YHWH asks His people why, when He has been faithful, they have continued to be rebellious. YHWH is using a covenant treaty pattern (i.e. Hittite Suzerain Treaties of the second millennium B.C., which also form the outline of the book of Deuteronomy and Joshua 24) to recall His faithful acts.

Special Topic: Hittite (Suzerain) Treaties

Special Topic: Stubbornness

entries.title: Micah 6:4 "I brought you up. . .Egypt"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:4 "I brought you up. . .Egypt" This refers to YHWH's promise to Abraham in Gen. 15:6 and relates to the events of the exodus. The exodus is the foundational act of YHWH's redemption in the history of national Israel (cf. Exod. 20:2; Deut. 5:6; 7:8). This event clearly showed YHWH's faithful commitment to His covenant responsibilities (i.e. Amos 2:10; 3:1; 9:7). God's grace came before the Mosaic law.

Special Topic: Characteristics of Israel's God (OT)

▣ "ransomed" This word literally means "to buy back" (BDB 804, KB 911, Qal PERFECT). It was used in the sense of buying someone back from slavery or a from being prisoner of war. This concept becomes a key theological term. The opposition idiom would be God "sold" them!

Special Topic: Ransom/Redeem

▣ "I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam" YHWH had provided the needed revelations and godly leadership, but His people had rebelled, even during the exodus. His people have a track record of rebellion (cf. Stephen's sermon in Acts 7).

Notice Miriam is mentioned in a parallel way to Moses and Aaron. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1214, says "Miriam, here, plays a role equal to her brothers."

Special Topic: Women in the Bible

Special Topic: Ways of Revelation

entries.title: Micah 6:5 "remember now"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:5 "remember now" This (BDB 269, KB 269) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. YHWH wants His covenant people to remember an earlier time of testing and revelation (i.e. Num. 22:5-6).

It is interesting that in the OT, YHWH is called on to forget (i.e. their sin), but His people to remember (His word)!

▣ "Balak. . .Balaam" This event is recorded in Numbers 22-25. See my exegetical notes there online, www.freebiblecommentary.org

▣ "Shittim" This was the last camping site of Israel before entering the Promised Land. It is also the scene of the sin of Israel with Moabite women (i.e. fertility worship, cf. Num. 33:49).

▣ "Gilgal" This was the first camping site within the Promised Land (cf. Joshua 4:19). Even in the midst of their sin and rebellion at Shittim, YHWH forgave them and brought them safely through the raging, flooding Jordan River into the Promised Land.

Taken together the mentioning of these two locations would imply the miraculous crossing of the Jordan River during its flooding season (cf. Joshua 3).

▣ "the righteous acts of the Lord" Righteousness is a key theological concept.

Special Topic: Righteousness

entries.title: Micah 6:6 "With what shall I come to the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:6 "With what shall I come to the Lord" This is a crucial question. Judah thought the sacrificial system (i.e. Lev. 1-7) was the key. The system was not the problem. It had been given by YHWH. The problem was ritual and liturgy without heart felt faith and worth, accompanied by a lifestyle that neglected and disregarded the other aspects of the Mosaic legislation. Judah took the system as the goal instead of a growing covenant love for God that issues in covenant love for His people (i.e. v. 8; 1 Sam. 15:22; Ps. 51:16-17; Prov. 21:3. The NT counterpoint would be Jesus' words in Matt. 22:36-40; Mark 12:28-34; Luke 10:25-28).

Think of what moderns bring to God and think they are accepted!

▣
NASB, REB  "the God on high"
NKJV, Peshitta  "the High God"
NRSV, JPSOA  "God on high"
TEV  "the God of heaven"
NJB  "God All-high"
LXX  "to my God Most HIgh"
NET  "the sovereign God"

This (BDB 43 CONSTRUCT BDB 928) is imagery for "the Most High God" or "exalted God" (cf. Ps. 99:2; 113:4; 38:6; Isa. 57:15). Here, it refers to YHWH, but not in a polytheistic pantheon. He is alone, unique. The only True God!

Special Topic: Monotheism

Special Topic: Names for Deity, A.

▣ "yearling calves" These were unblemished calves (characteristic markings of the species) used for sacrifice from the age of eight days to one year (cf. Lev. 9:3 and 22:27).

entries.title: Micah 6:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:6-7 In verses 6-7 the literary form of diatribe (i.e. a supposed objector) is used. There is a series of questions by the covenant people. YHWH answers these in v. 8. The prophet uses a supposed collective person to voice the false views which were commonly held by the people of Judah. They thought YHWH was being unfair to them and that He only wanted more sacrifices.

There is a good discussion in Ancient Israel, pp. 454-456, by Roland deVaux about the texts in the OT that seem to reject sacrifices as the will of God.

Special Topic: YHWH's Covenant Requirements of Israel

entries.title: Micah 6:7 "in thousands of rams. . .rivers of oil"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:7 "in thousands of rams. . .rivers of oil" The people are

  1. charging YHWH of being unreasonable in His requirements. However, He never asked for these things. They reflect pagan worship practices.
  2. on some national occasions large numbers of sacrifices are given (i.e. dedication of Solomon's temple, i.e. 1 Kgs. 8:63).

Could this representative speaker be talking of an event of national repentance (i.e. ritual sacrifice)?

▣ "first-born. . .fruit of my body" Is this a purposeful distortion (i.e. hyperbole) or a sincere misunderstanding of Genesis 22 or Exod. 13:2-12? There are several places in the Mosaic Law where human sacrifice is condemned (cf. Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5; Deut. 12:31; 18:10; Ps. 106:37; Jer. 7:31).

It is possible that YHWH's people had become so spiritually confused that they attempted to worship Him in the form of Molech, the fertility fire god of Ammon (cf. Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5; 1 Kgs. 11:7; 2 Kgs. 3:27; 16:3; 17:17; 21:6; 23:10; Jer. 32:35; Amos 5:26; Acts 7:43).

YHWH's people attempted to save the nation by offering an innocent one ("child"). In some way they had logically extended the sacrificial system (cf. Lev. 1-7) in an inappropriate direction. However, it is this same concept that lies behind Genesis 22 and Calvary (cf. Isa. 53; Mark 10:45; 2 Cor. 5:21).

Special Topic: Molech

entries.title: Micah 6:8 "He has told you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:8 "He has told you" The VERB (BDB 616, KB 665) is a Hiphil PERFECT and may reflect Micah 6:4. God had provided a revelation of His character and will (esp. as it related to sacrifice, cf. 1 Sam. 15:22; Ps. 51:16-17; Isa. 1:11-17; Hosea 6:5-6). This verse seems to reflect a comment of Micah.

▣ "soul" See Special Topic: Nephesh

▣ "O, man" This VOCATIVE is addressing the idolatrous covenant people of Judah. This verse is not addressing how Gentiles might be saved (i.e. works righteousness), but how covenant people must live in grateful response to YHWH's forgiveness (which in the OT was symbolized as the sacrifice of an innocent animal, cf. John 1:29; 2 Cor. 5:21). For a good brief discussion of this topic see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 336-337.

▣ "what is good" This verse is the most well known saying of the book of Micah. It refers to the priority of loving, interpersonal relationships on a high level of care and love (cf. Ps. 14:1,3; 37:3; 51:17; Hosea 12:6 and described in Ps. 15:2-5), not cultic performance (i.e. sacrifice) only (cf. Isa. 1:13; Amos 5:21-23).

This verse is a wonderful definition of what OT "good" (BDB 373 II) is in YHWH's eyes (cf. Micah 3:2; Isa. 1:17; 5:20; Amos 5:14-15). This definition of "good" matches Rom. 8:28, explained in v. 29 as Christlikeness.

▣ "require" This VERB (BDB 205, KB 233) is a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, which represents continuous action. The term means "to demand" or "ask for" (i.e. Deut. 18:19; 23:21).

▣ "justice" In this context "justice" (BDB 1048, see Special Topic: Justice) refers to social fairness, which is discussed in Micah 6:9-11. The OT knows no distinction between the secular and the sacred! All of life is sacred! See note at Micah 3:1.

There is a series of three Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS:

  1. "Do justice" (BDB 793, KB 889; see Special Topic: Justice)
  2. "Love kindness" (BDB 12, KB 17; see Special Topic: Lovingkindness)
  3. "Walk humbly" (BDB 229, KB 246; see Special Topic: The Path, The Way)

Biblical faith affects every aspect of daily life. Faith is a lifestyle, not just a theology or creed (i.e. Eph. 1:4; 2:10. The divine covenant gift of eternal life (i.e. the restoration of the image and likeness of God damaged in the fall) has observable characteristics (both in relation to God and other humans). This verse is one of the best in the OT describing these characteristics.

▣ "love kindness" This is the powerful covenant word hesed (BDB 338). It refers to YHWH's covenant loyalty. It reflects His sacrificial, no-strings-attached, covenant love. I think this term, in many ways, is analogous in meaning to the NT agapē.

Special Topic: Lovingkindness (hesed)

Special Topic: Love (agapē)

▣ "walk humbly" This is an acknowledgment of

  1. human need (i.e. possible meaning of this rare word "humble" (BDB 857, KB 1039, INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, cf. Prov. 11:2, found only here)
  2. human lifestyle guided by YHWH's revelation (i.e. Mosaic covenant requirements)

Ritual without the proper attitude (cf. Isa. 29:13 vs. 57:15 and 66:2d) is an abomination (cf. 1 Sam. 15:22; Matt. 23:23).

"Walk" in the Bible is

  1. imagery of fellowship with someone (i.e. Gen. 5:24; 6:9; Job 34:8; Ps. 1:1; Mal. 2:6)
  2. imagery for daily living (cf. Eph. 4:1,17; 5:2,15)

Biblical faith is daily (not weekly or annually), personal relationship directed toward YHWH and other human beings! Biblical faith has observable characteristics. It is both what not to do but also what to do!

Special Topic: The Path, The Way

entries.title: Micah 6:9 "The voice of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:9 "The voice of the Lord" The message begins in line 3 and continues to Micah 6:16. This word "voice" (BDB 876) is used several times for YHWH speaking (cf. Exod. 19:19; 1 Kgs. 19:13; Isa. 6:8; Ezek. 10:5). The NJB has "He thunders to the city," which alludes to Exod. 19:13,16.

For "Lord" see Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

▣ "the city" This refers to Jerusalem, the special place where YHWH caused His name to dwell (cf. Deut. 12:5,11), the location of the temple.

Special Topic: Jerusalem

▣
NASB, NRSV  "it is sound wisdom to fear Your name"
NKJV  "wisdom shall see Your name"
TEV  "it is wise to fear the Lord"
REB  "(the fear of his name brings success)"
JPSOA  "then will your name achieve wisdom"
LXX  "and he shall save those who fear his
  name"
Peshitta  "preaching doctrine to those who revere
  his name"
NET  "(it is wise to respect your authority)"

The MT has "and sound wisdom will see your name" (NKJV).

The phrase is a comment from Micah or a later editorial addition (omitted in JB and NJB). It was a wisdom saying. The NRSV, NET, and REB put it in brackets.

The Hebrew term (BDB 444) translated "sound wisdom" is a technical term used in wisdom literature (see Special Topic: Wisdom Literature) for sound and effective godly wisdom (cf. Job 11:6; 12:16; 26:3; Prov. 2:7; 3:21; 8:14; 18:1; Isa. 28:29).

The term "fear" is an emendation from the Hebrew "to see" (BDB 906, cf. NKJV) following the Septuagint (BDB 431), which fits the context better and is found in NASB, RSV, NRSV, TEV, NEB, REB, NIV.

  1. "see" ‒ MT (BDB 906 ‒ ראה)
  2. "fear" ‒ LXX (BDB 431 ‒ ירא)

The inflected forms use the same consonants but different vowels.

Special Topic: Fear

The word "name" stands for the person of God (BDB 1027, cf. Gen. 4:26; 12:8; 13:4; 21:33; Acts 7:59; 9:14,21; 22:16; Rom. 10:9-13; 1 Cor. 1:2; 2 Tim. 2:22).

Special Topic: "The Name" of YHWH

▣ "Hear" This (BDB 1033, KB 1570) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. This may be a textual marker of a transition to a new context (cf. Micah 1:1; 3:1; 6:1).

Special Topic: Listen/Hear (shema)

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta, LXX  "O tribe"
NKJV  "the Rod"
REB  "your tribe"
JPSOA  "O scepter"
NET  "O nation"

The Masoretic Text has "rod."

The Hebrew root can mean

  1. rod (Num. 17:18,21,23,25; Isa. 10:5)
  2. staff (Gen. 38:18; Exod. 4:17)
  3. branch (Ezek. 19:11,12,14)
  4. tribe (Exod. 31:2; Lev. 24:11; Num. 1:4)

YHWH addresses His people's social exploitations of the poor and needy covenantal brothers and sisters (cf. Micah 6:12 and the book of Amos).

▣
NASB  "Who has appointed its time"
NKJV  "Who has appointed it"
NRSV  ". . .an assembly of the city"
TEV  "you people who have assembled in the city"
NJB  ". . .of assembled citizens"
LXX  "Who shall order the city?"
Peshitta  "who testifies against you"

The NASB and NKJV follow the Hebrew text while the NRSV, TEV, NET, and NJB choose an emendation (not in the LXX). The UBS Text Project, p. 324, gives "appoint" a "C" rating, meaning the committee could not decide.

If the MT is followed it speaks of YHWH's sovereign establishment of Jerusalem and His judgment of it!

6:10
NASB  "Is there yet a man in the wicked house"
NKJV  "Are there yet the treasures of wickedness"
NRSV  "Can I forget the treasures of wickedness"
TEV  "In the houses of evil people and treasures"
NJB  "Can I overlook the false measure"
Peshitta  "For there is still fire in the house of the wicked"
LXX  "Is there not fire, and the house of the wicked
  heaping up wicked treasures"

The second word in the MT is uncertain:

  1. האשׁ ‒ Is a man? (NASB)
  2. הישׁ ‒ Is there? (NKJV)
  3. האשׁה ‒ Will I forget? (NRSV)
  4. האשׂה ‒ Will I support? (NJB)

The context of false scales (i.e. Micah 6:10-11) seems to demand revocalization (change of the vowels but not consonants) of the Masoretic Text to commercial imagery (cf. Micah 6:11). The MT is in the form of a question which expects a "yes" answer.

entries.title: Micah 6:10-11 "short measure. . .wicked scales. . .deceptive weights"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:10-11 "short measure. . .wicked scales. . .deceptive weights" The MT of Micah 6:11 is in the form of a question, but expects a "no" answer. These are examples of commercial cheating (cf. Hosea 12:7; Amos 8:5).

For a full discussion of Hebrew weights and measures, see Special Topic: ANE Weights and Volumes

6:11
NASB, MT  "Can I justify"
NKJV  "shall I count pure"
NRSV  "can I tolerate"
TEV  "how can I forgive"
NJB, REB  "can I connive"
NET  "can I condone"
JPSOA  "shall he be acquited"
JPSOA (footnote)  "will I acquit him"
Peshitta  "how can they justify themselves"
LXX  "shall the wicked be justified"

The textual issue is obvious. Who is speaking, YHWH or the prophet? The wicked merchants are the ones being condemned!

entries.title: Micah 6:12 "the rich"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:12 "the rich" Micah's message is addressed to the privileged, powerful, influential, and wealthy covenant citizens. It is very similar to that of Amos. Notice how line 2 and line 3 are parallel. All three lines are a summary of Micah 6:9-10 and the opposite of Micah 6:8.

Notice the words which relate to lying, wealthy, covenant brothers.

Special Topic: Wealth

entries.title: Micah 6:13-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:13-15 YHWH will judge the people of Jerusalem by siege and exile. All their ill-gotten gains will be enjoyed by foreign invaders. Notice the reason for these actions is not the weakness of YHWH in protecting His people from foreign gods, but His people's sin (cf. Micah 6:13b,16)! There are consequences for covenant disobedience (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28)!

6:13
NASB, NKJV  "I will make you sick"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta  "I have begun to strike you sore"
JPSOA  "I, in turn, have beaten you sure"
NET  "I will strike your brutality"

The NASB and NKJV follow the MT; the others follow the Septuagint, Peshitta, and Vulgate. The UBS Text Project, p. 327, gives he MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "Desolating you" This term (BDB 1030, KB 1563, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) is found in many Akkadian medical texts translated "paralyze," "numb" and "lame." Therefore, the first two lines of poetry in Micah 6:13 have parallel medical imagery related to sinning covenant people.

6:14
NASB  "your vileness will be in your midst"
NKJV  "hunger shall be in your midst"
NRSV  "there shall be a gnawing hunger within you"
TEV  "you will still be hungry"
JPSOA  "there is a gnawing at your vitals"
REB  "your food will lie heavy in your stomach"
LXX  "it shall grow dark within you"
Peshitta  "dysentery shall be in the midst of you"
NET  "even if they have the strength"

The problem is the term "vileness" or "empty by hunger" (BDB 445). Its meaning is uncertain. It is used only here in the OT.

  1. KB (446) has "to be dirty." (Arabic root "wash dirt away")
  2. The Peshitta translates it as "filth" (i.e. dysentery)
  3. LXX has "darkness"
  4. The NET Bible, p. 1629, #6, assumes an emendation, "and [if] there is strength inside you"
    1. MT, וישׁחך, "and your hunger"
    2. וישׁ כח ‒ "and (if) there is strength inside you"

It is also uncertain if it refers to (1) an individual or (2) the sinful society.

The ill gotten gain from the poor will backfire on them.

▣
NASB  "You will try to remove for safekeeping"
NKJV  "You may carry some away"
NRSV  "you shall put away"
TEV  "you will carry things off"
NJB  "you will store up"
NET  "to overtake some prey, you will not
  be able to carry it away"

The VERB "remove" (BDB 690 I, KB 744, Hiphil [this form is used everywhere also in the OT of moving a boundary stone] JUSSIVE) is understood to be an attempt to hide possessions or valuables for safe keeping, but it will not be effective! The invaders will find all the wealth and hidden food and take it!

The next line of poetry uses the VERB "preserve" or "save" (BDB 812, KB 930, Hiphil IMPERFECT), which was used in Isa. 5:29 of a lioness hiding and licking her food to preserve it. The NKJV seems to follow this scavenger imagery, as does the NET Bible.

Jewish tradition interprets this as referring to the attempt to hide their young children, but they will be killed by the invader's sword.

entries.title: Micah 6:15 "sow but. . .not reap"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:15 "sow but. . .not reap" This is part of the curse for breaking the covenant (cf. Deut. 28:30 ff). All of the wealthy people's economic plans will be thwarted by the invaders.

▣ "will not anoint yourself with oil" Olive oil had many purposes in ANE. One of them was to rub on the skin in preparation of a social event. It was a symbol of happiness and joy. The lack of oil was seen as a divine judgment (cf. Deut. 28:40).

Special Topic: Anointing in the Bible

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB   "grapes"
NKJV, Peshitta   "sweet wine"
TEV, LXX   "wine"

This is the Hebrew term for "new wine" (BDB 440).

Special Topic: Wine and Strong Drink

entries.title: Micah 6:16 "Omri"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:16 "Omri" This was a politically effective king of Israel (i.e. 876-869 B.C., cf. 1 Kgs. 16:21-28). His name became the common name for the Northern Ten Tribes in the Assyrian records (i.e. "House of Omri"). This title became an idiom for their godless living. It came to characterize Judah also in v. 6, line 3 (cf. Micah 1:9, i.e. 2 Kgs. 17:19,22)!

Special Topic: Kings of the Divided Kingdom

▣ "Ahab" This is Omri's son who married Jezebel, who brought numerous prophets of Ba'al and Asherah into Samarian society (i.e. 869-850 B.C., cf. 1 Kgs. 16:29-34; 18; 21:25).

▣
NASB  "derision"
NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, Peshitta, LXX  "hissing"
TEV  "despise"
NJB  "a laughing-stock"
REB  "horror"

This is the Hebrew word "hissing" (BDB 1056), which was a cultural way of showing disgust and rejection (cf. 2 Chr. 29:8; Jer. 18:16; 19:8; 25:9,18; 29:18; 51:37). See full note on physical gestures of contempt at Lam. 2:15 online.

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "you will bear the reproach of My
  people"
NRSV  "so you shall bear the scorn of my people"
TEV  "People everywhere will treat you with
  contempt"
NJB, JPSOA  "hence you will endure the scorn of other
  peoples"
LXX, JPSOA  "and you shall receive reproaches of
  peoples"

The different translation options are based on:

  1. The MT, "My people" ‒ NASB, NKJV, NRSV, REB, Peshitta, עםי
  2. The Septuagint, "of the peoples" ‒ RSV, TEV, NJB, JPSOA, NET, עמים

The UBS Text Project, p. 328, gives "my people" a "B" rating.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why did God bring His people to court?
  2. Why are Micah 6:6-7 so upsetting?
  3. Is God concerned with our business life?

entries.title: Micah 7:1 "Woe is me!"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:1 "Woe is me!" This is an individual lament (BDB 47), although at times it moves into the area of a corporate plea. This is a common literary technique of the Psalms (cf. Ps. 5; 13; 22; 55; 71).

It is uncertain who is speaking:

  1. the prophet himself
  2. the prophet as YHWH's spokesperson
  3. the prophet on behalf of the godly remnant
  4. Samaria (JPSOA footnote, "the speaker is FEMININE, cf. Micah 6:16). Remember, Isaiah and Micah are 8th century prophets. Assyria was the immediate threat.
▣
NASB  "I am like the fruit pickers"
NKJV, REB, Peshitta  "For I am like those who gather
  summer fruit"
NRSV  "For I have become like one who, after
  the summer fruit has been gathered"
TEV  "I am like a hungry person who finds
  no fruit"
NJB  "a harvester in summer time"
JPSOA  "I am become like leavings of a fig
  harvest"
LXX  "I have become like one gathering
  stubble at the harvest"

The NASB has left out the term "summer" (BDB 884) which denotes "heat." This gathering is not the initial harvest, but the last pickings of the post-harvest season. YHWH waited and waited for fruit, but there was never a harvest (cf. Isaiah 5)!

▣ "Like the fruit-pickers and the grape gatherers" Micah craves righteousness (or a righteous people or righteous leadership, i.e. Micah 7:3) as a hungry man craves food (cf. Matt. 5:6). The concept of righteousness as food is found throughout the Bible (cf. Amos 6:12; John 15:1-8; Phil. 1:11; Gal. 5:23).

The Jewish Publication Society of America (JPSOA) says Micah 7:1 refers to Samaria. They search for food, but cannot find it because of

  1. the siege
  2. YHWH's famine, cf. Deuteronomy 27-28)

The JPSOA continues this thought through Micah 7:7.

However, I think this context relates to Jerusalem.

  1. in one sense they are too late (i.e. the harvest of their unrighteousness has occurred—exile)
  2. in another sense they are too early (i.e. the promise of restoration in the future has not yet come)

▣ "first ripe fig, which I crave" These early figs were very sweet and sought after. They first appeared in June, although, the major harvest did not occur until August. Micah (as YHWH's spokesman) is searching for righteousness as a man longs for these first figs.
